q: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood low in oxygen out to the lungs?
o: The left ventricle
The right ventricle
The left atrium
The right atrium
e: The ventricles are the main pumps: the right sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen, the left sends oxygen-rich blood to the whole body. The atria collect blood arriving at the heart.

q: Where does each heartbeat start?
o: At the sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium
In the motor cortex, as with skeletal muscle
At the atrioventricular (AV) node in the ventricles
In the wall of the left ventricle
e: The SA node is the heart's pacemaker. The impulse spreads across the atria and then passes through the AV node into the ventricles. Cardiac muscle is not under conscious control.

q: A client's heart rate is 12 beats higher than usual at a familiar steady workload. They have no chest discomfort, dizziness or palpitations. What is the most accurate reading?
o: Heavy overreaching, so cut the rest of the week's training
A warning sign, so stop the session and refer them now
Ordinary causes such as heat, poor sleep, illness or caffeine
Training has raised their maximum heart rate this month
e: A higher heart rate at a familiar workload has many common causes, including heat, dehydration, illness, poor sleep, stress, caffeine, new medication or lost fitness. Heavy overreaching more often lowers it. Stop and refer only if it comes with warning symptoms.

q: A trained client rests at 50 beats a minute and an untrained one at 72, with the same resting cardiac output. What mainly explains the trained client's lower rate?
o: Less blood volume to pump around the body
A larger stroke volume and stronger vagal tone
Arteries that stay permanently dilated
A higher maximum heart rate built by training
e: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, so a bigger stroke volume delivers the same output in fewer beats. Training changes maximum heart rate little.

q: Roughly how much blood does an adult hold?
o: About 10 litres
About 15 litres
About 2 litres
About 5 litres
e: An adult holds about 5 litres of blood, which carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste and heat.

q: Which part of the blood carries glucose, fats, proteins, hormones and clotting factors?
o: Plasma
Platelets
Red blood cells
White blood cells
e: Plasma is the fluid part of blood and carries glucose, fats, proteins, hormones and clotting factors. The cells in it are red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

q: In which vessels are oxygen, nutrients and waste exchanged with the tissues?
o: Veins
Capillaries
Venules
Arterioles
e: Capillaries are the smallest vessels and form the fine network where exchange happens. Arterioles branch off arteries; venules collect blood on the way back.

q: After hard intervals, an older client on blood-pressure medication wants to stop dead and stand still. What do you advise, and why?
o: Taper off gradually, so the muscle pump keeps blood moving back from the legs
Sit down straight away, because resting clears lactate fastest
Stand still until the heart rate settles, since movement strains the heart
Stretch statically on the floor, to prevent next-day soreness
e: Contracting leg muscles pump blood back through the veins. Stopping dead switches the pump off while the heart is still racing, so blood pools in the legs and can cause dizziness, especially in older adults and anyone on blood-pressure medication.

q: In the UK, which clinic reading counts as high blood pressure?
o: 130/85 or more
160/100 or more
120/80 or more
140/90 or more
e: UK clinic readings of 140/90 or more count as high, or 135/85 or more at home. 120/80 is the upper edge of normal.

q: A client's home monitor averages 137/86 over a week. How does that compare with UK thresholds?
o: It is normal, since only a diastolic over 90 counts
It counts as high, since the home threshold is 135/85
It is normal, since it is under the clinic threshold of 140/90
It is an emergency, so they must stop exercising today
e: Home readings use a lower threshold, 135/85, than clinic readings, 140/90. High blood pressure alone is not an emergency.

q: A client at rest is breathing 22 times a minute. How do clinical sources classify that?
o: Normal, since the adult range runs 12 to 30
Tachypnoea, since clinical sources use above 20
Normal, since NASM's cut-off is above 24
Bradypnoea, since it is slower than exercise breathing
e: Normal adult resting breathing is about 12 to 20 breaths a minute. Clinical sources call anything above 20 tachypnoea; NASM uses above 24. Bradypnoea is below 8.

q: A healthy runner asks whether nasal strips will improve their performance. What is the accurate answer?
o: No: at sea level, breathing does not limit healthy people
Only for efforts above the second ventilatory threshold
Yes: breathing rate is the main limit on hard running
Yes: they deepen each breath and so shrink the dead space
e: The lungs can raise their output enormously even at maximum effort, which is why nasal strips do nothing. Breathing can be the limit in lung disease and in some elite endurance athletes.

q: Which two energy pathways are anaerobic?
o: Glycolysis and the oxidative system
All three pathways
ATP-PCr and glycolysis
ATP-PCr and the oxidative system
e: ATP-PCr and glycolysis need no oxygen. The oxidative system is aerobic. Together they form the bioenergetic continuum.

q: When one energy system leads, what are the other two doing?
o: Switched off until the leading system runs out
Producing lactate as a by-product
Being held back by the nervous system
Still running, because all three run all the time
e: All three pathways run all the time. The bioenergetic continuum only says which one leads.

q: Which energy system responds first at the start of any activity, whatever the intensity?
o: Whichever matches the intensity
The oxidative system
ATP-PCr
Glycolysis
e: ATP-PCr is the fastest system, so it covers the first seconds of anything before another system takes over.

q: For roughly how long can the ATP-PCr system power a maximal effort before another system takes over?
o: About 10 seconds
About 2 seconds
About 2 minutes
About 45 seconds
e: Phosphocreatine remakes ATP in a single step, which powers short maximal efforts such as heavy lifts and short sprints for about 10 seconds.

q: What does glycolysis yield from one glucose molecule?
o: A net 36 ATP and two pyruvate
A net two ATP and two pyruvate
A net two ATP and two lactate
About 30 ATP and carbon dioxide
e: Glycolysis breaks down glucose without oxygen for a net two ATP and two pyruvate. Pyruvate becomes lactate when it is produced faster than the cell can use it.

q: Why do most gym sets stress glycolysis more than the other energy systems?
o: Glycolysis is the only system that runs under load
Resistance work runs on fat, which glycolysis burns
A set of 8 to 12 falls inside its 30-to-60-second window
A set of 8 to 12 lasts under the 10 seconds it covers
e: Glycolysis lasts only about 30 to 60 seconds at high intensity, and a typical set of 8 to 12 falls inside that window.

q: On modern estimates, roughly how many ATP come from burning one glucose molecule with oxygen?
o: About 2
About 30 to 32
About 100
About 38
e: Older figures, including NASM's, give 36 to 38; around 30 to 32 is the modern estimate. Either way it is about fifteen times the yield of glycolysis alone.

q: Why is the oxidative system the slowest to get going?
o: Breathing and blood flow take time to rise
It produces the least ATP of the three systems
It can only burn protein, which is slow to break down
It only starts once phosphocreatine has run out
e: The oxidative system needs oxygen delivered in line with demand, and that takes time. It is the slowest to start but produces by far the most energy.

t: How the body keeps up with demand
q: Which fuel can the body break down both with and without oxygen?
o: Protein
Phosphocreatine
Carbohydrate
Fat
e: Carbohydrate is the only fuel the body can break down both with and without oxygen. Fat is slow: it has to be released, transported and broken down in the mitochondria, which is why it never fuels a sprint.

t: How the body keeps up with demand
q: What happens to muscle protein synthesis during a hard session?
o: It falls, as building protein switches off to save ATP
It rises in step with how acidic the muscle becomes
It stays unchanged until the last set is finished
It peaks, because the muscle is under the heaviest load
e: As the cell's energy charge falls, pathways that use ATP for building switch off to save it for contraction. Synthesis rebounds after the effort and stays raised for a day or more.

q: For a maximal effort, modern measurements put the point where aerobic and anaerobic energy are equal at about:
o: 10 seconds
2 to 4 minutes
75 seconds
10 minutes
e: The older table puts the crossover at 2 to 4 minutes, which understates the aerobic share. Modern measurements put it at about 75 seconds.

q: A football coach says the sport is all sprints, so aerobic training is a waste of time. What is the better view?
o: Repeated sprints need an aerobic base as well
Aerobic training slows sprinters, so it should be avoided
Correct: anything built from sprints is purely anaerobic
Aerobic work matters only for players who run over 10 km
e: Use the duration of the working effort, not the name of the sport. Intermittent team sports need an aerobic base for repeated sprints, as well as the short-burst systems.

t: Applying the three systems to programme design
q: Which training approach best develops the glycolytic system?
o: Maximal efforts of under 10 seconds with long rests
Intervals that balance work with short recoveries
Long, continuous work at a moderate intensity
Static holds of several minutes at a light load
e: Glycolytic work of about 30 to 60 seconds with short rests keeps you in that system. ATP-PCr wants short maximal work with long rests; the oxidative system wants long moderate work.

t: Applying the three systems to programme design
q: A client doing heavy triples near their maximum wants to cut rests to 45 seconds to keep their heart rate up. What is the likely effect?
o: It stops being strength training and becomes pure cardio
No change, as phosphocreatine is fully back within 30 seconds
Later sets get lighter, so it builds a little less strength
More strength, because the extra fatigue drives adaptation
e: Phosphocreatine is remade slowly, with most back within about three minutes. Cut the rest and you lift less in later sets, so the session builds a little less strength and size, though it is still strength training. Heavy work near maximum wants 3 to 5 minutes.

t: Applying the three systems to programme design
q: A general client who only runs asks whether they need any other kind of training. What is the best answer?
o: Yes: strength work preserves muscle and bone
No: adding strength work would blunt their endurance
Yes: they need three kinds of session in equal numbers
No: running already trains all three energy systems equally
e: Each system buys something the others do not, so someone who only runs has a real gap. Balance does not mean equal sessions: strength can be held on one session a week once built.

q: During a maximal effort to exhaustion, what happens to ATP and phosphocreatine?
o: Both fall steadily together from the first second
ATP runs out first, then phosphocreatine follows
Phosphocreatine rises to replace the ATP being spent
ATP barely moves while phosphocreatine falls away
e: ATP is defended and phosphocreatine is spent to defend it. Only when phosphocreatine runs out does ATP collapse, and exhaustion follows at once.

q: Which is a cause of fatigue in long, moderate exercise rather than in short, hard efforts?
o: Carbohydrate running out in muscle, then liver
Hydrogen ions building up and raising acidity
Phosphocreatine running out within seconds
ATP collapsing once phosphocreatine is spent
e: Long moderate work ends through carbohydrate running out, calcium leaking away and heat building up. Phosphocreatine loss, falling ATP and rising acidity end short, hard efforts.

q: A client says the burn in hard sets is lactic acid, and that it is also why they are sore the next day. What is accurate?
o: Neither is caused by lactate
Both are caused by lactate
Only the burn is caused by lactate
Only the soreness is caused by lactate
e: Hydrogen ions come from splitting ATP at a high rate, not from making lactate, which actually lets glycolysis keep running. Lactate is gone within about an hour; next-day soreness is eccentric muscle damage.

q: A HIIT class is advertised as burning calories for hours afterwards through the afterburn. What is accurate?
o: It is real, but typically only 6 to 15% of the session's cost
The afterburn typically doubles the calorie cost of the session
There is no afterburn: oxygen use returns to rest at once
The afterburn follows only long, steady, low-intensity cardio
e: EPOC, the raised oxygen use after hard exercise, is real. It is often sold as a major source of calories burned, and the evidence is against that.

q: Why are Type I fibres the endurance fibres?
o: They burn fat without needing oxygen
They are rich in mitochondria
They run glycolysis faster than Type II
They hold the most phosphocreatine
e: The oxidative pathway runs in the mitochondria, the parts of the cell that make energy using oxygen. Aerobic work builds new mitochondria, which slows their loss with age.

q: A client says fasted cardio burns more fat. What is the accurate reply?
o: Only if the session stays in the fat-burning zone
More fat in the session, the same fat loss over weeks
No: fasting stops the body using fat as a fuel
Yes: it roughly doubles fat loss over a few weeks
e: Fasted cardio burns more fat during the session but gives the same fat loss over weeks. Over weeks, fat loss follows energy balance, not the fuel mix of the session.

q: In most people, around what intensity does carbohydrate overtake fat as the main fuel?
o: About 40 to 45% of VO2max
About 25 to 30% of VO2max
About 60 to 65% of VO2max
About 85 to 90% of VO2max
e: That point is the crossover. At 25% of VO2max about 90% of energy comes from fat, at 65% roughly half and half, and at 85% about 75% from carbohydrate. Training shifts the crossover towards fat.

t: Muscle glycogen and liver glycogen do different jobs
q: Why can muscle glycogen not be used to keep blood glucose up?
o: Muscle stores too little glycogen to spare any
Muscle glycogen is converted to fat before it is used
Blood glucose is kept up by fat released from fat tissue
Muscle lacks the enzyme that frees glucose for export
e: Only the liver can release glucose into the blood. Whatever glycogen a muscle breaks down, it burns itself. Fat is fuel, but it is not glucose.

t: Muscle glycogen and liver glycogen do different jobs
q: A client doing hard endurance sessions asks when glycogen in the working muscles starts to run low. What is the best answer?
o: Not until about 5 hours at any intensity
After about 45 minutes, later in intervals
After about 20 minutes, whatever the pace
After roughly 90 minutes to 2 hours
e: Glycogen in the working muscles runs low after roughly 90 minutes to 2 hours of hard endurance work, sooner in intervals. It lasts much longer at an easy pace.

q: What does indirect calorimetry measure to estimate metabolic rate?
o: Heart rate against workload
Heat given off in a sealed chamber
Oxygen use
Change in core body temperature
e: Indirect calorimetry estimates metabolic rate from oxygen use and is by far the most common method. Direct calorimetry measures heat in a chamber and is expensive and impractical.

q: Why can measuring either heat or oxygen use give the metabolic rate?
o: Both are read from heart rate, which tracks metabolism
Heat comes only from fat and oxygen only from carbohydrate
Oxygen use is always exactly twice the heat produced
They measure two ends of the same reaction
e: Burning food follows one reaction. Direct calorimetry measures the heat; indirect calorimetry measures the oxygen used. All metabolism ends as heat.

q: A client asks whether getting fitter is worth it for their health. Each extra MET of fitness is linked with roughly what change in all-cause mortality?
o: No change once a basic level is reached
About 12 to 13% lower, with no limit seen
About 1 to 2% lower, levelling off early
About 50% lower for each MET gained
e: One MET is 3.5 ml of oxygen per kilogram per minute, roughly sitting still. Each extra MET of fitness goes with roughly 12 to 13% lower all-cause mortality, with no upper limit seen (well supported, observational).

q: Two rival runners differed by 16% in VO2max, yet their best mile times differed by under 8 seconds. What does this show?
o: VO2max predicts performance less than people think
Mile times depend on VO2max and nothing else
The runner with the lower VO2max must have trained harder
VO2max tests are too inaccurate to compare two runners
e: Endurance performance rests on VO2max, the lactate threshold and economy. A VO2max test lasts minutes and says nothing about resistance to fatigue.

q: In steady-state exercise, an RER of 0.85 indicates:
o: Half fat, half carbohydrate
Almost all from fat
Mostly from protein
Almost all from carbohydrate
e: RER is carbon dioxide produced divided by oxygen used. 0.70 means all fat, 0.85 half and half, and 1.00 all carbohydrate.

q: During hard sprint intervals a client's RER reads 1.1. What does that mean?
o: The analyser is faulty, since RER cannot pass 1.0
They have switched to protein as the main fuel
Carbon dioxide from buffering acid is pushing it up
They are burning more than 100% carbohydrate
e: RER reflects fuel use only in steady-state exercise. In sprints, carbon dioxide from buffering acid pushes it above 1.0, which does not mean more than 100% carbohydrate.

q: A client trains hard with you three times a week but sleeps five hours and eats little after sessions. Progress is slow. What is the best framing?
o: The sessions are too easy, so raise the intensity
Food and sleep matter only for competitive athletes
Adaptation happens in recovery, so sleep and food count
Progress is slow for everyone in the first year
e: Adaptation is a recovery event, not a training event. Training creates the demand; sleep, food and time create the response.

q: Why does treating the workout as the whole job fall short?
o: The session is one hour of 168; most change happens outside it
Glycogen is fully restored within minutes of a session
Sessions burn too few calories to be worth planning at all
Muscle protein synthesis stops as soon as the session ends
e: Resting metabolism and everyday movement make up most energy use, glycogen is restored over hours, and protein synthesis runs for a day or more. The trainer's job is the design of the week.

t: Sitting, standing and the shape of the day
q: A desk worker says their 30-minute evening workout cancels out a day of sitting. What is accurate?
o: No amount of exercise can offset long periods of sitting
Not at 30 minutes; about an hour a day appears to
Only a standing desk removes the risk that sitting brings
Correct: any daily workout removes the risk of sitting
e: High volumes of activity, about an hour a day of at least moderate intensity, appear to cancel the mortality risk of long sitting. Few clients do that much, so for most, sitting is a separate risk worth reducing.

t: Sitting, standing and the shape of the day
q: A client wants to sit less. How should you set the goal?
o: Measure their sitting split and shift it, say 70/30 to 65/35
Ban sitting at work entirely until the habit is broken
Set a target matched to an ideal split for their age
Tell them to sit less and check in at the end of the month
e: A small, specific, trackable change beats "sit less", which has no finish line. The client plays against their own last number rather than an ideal.

q: Work travel will cut a client's training to one or two sessions a week for three months. What best protects their fitness?
o: Switch to light daily circuits in the hotel room
Stop completely and rebuild when travel ends
Keep the intensity; frequency and volume can drop
Keep the volume by making each session longer and easier
e: When training has to be cut, keep the intensity (fairly well supported). Endurance can be held on about two sessions a week and strength on one session with one hard set per exercise.

q: A dieting client wants to add a lot of high-volume cardio to speed fat loss. What mix do you suggest?
o: Two long cardio sessions a week, lifting stopped
Resistance work only, with no cardio at all
Daily long cardio sessions and no resistance work at all
Frequent, moderate cardio alongside resistance training
e: In a calorie deficit, a lot of high-volume cardio adds to muscle breakdown, so frequent, moderate cardio alongside resistance training is the better mix.

q: Why does diabetes guidance say not to go more than two days without activity?
o: Insulin medication stops working without exercise
Blood glucose rises sharply on the third rest day
Muscle stays more insulin-sensitive for a day or two
GLUT4 transporters are all lost after two days
e: Part of training's effect is acute: working muscle takes up glucose without insulin, and it stays more sensitive to insulin for a day or two afterwards. The rest is chronic: more GLUT4 and more muscle.

q: A client with type 2 diabetes asks what their training is actually for. What is the best answer?
o: Burning off the day's sugar
Replacing their medication
Raising resting metabolic rate
Raising insulin sensitivity
e: For type 2 diabetes, raising insulin sensitivity (lowering insulin resistance) is the goal, and training is the lever. Medication decisions belong to the doctor.

q: A client says they are an ectomorph, so they cannot build muscle and need a special programme. What is the accurate reply?
o: Ectomorphs should train only once a week to recover
Ectomorphs need very high reps to grow any muscle
Body types do not predict how anyone responds to training
Correct: ectomorphs have a much faster metabolic rate
e: Somatotypes are a descriptive 1940s scheme. Most people do not fit one type cleanly, and the evidence is against it predicting metabolic rate or training response.

q: What is the somatotype scheme reasonably used for?
o: Setting the client's daily calorie target
Choosing the client's rep ranges and sets
Opening a conversation about why people differ
Predicting the client's metabolic rate
e: Use it to start a conversation, not to decide a programme. Measure the person in front of you.

q: Why does a programme produce lasting change when a single session does not?
o: Only repeated signals change what the muscle builds
Each session adds a fixed amount of new muscle protein
A single session damages muscle that takes weeks to heal
Change only begins once twelve sessions have been done
e: Muscle plasticity works by changing which genes the muscle switches on. One session changes nothing lasting; repeated signals change what it builds. That is the mechanism under the overload principle.

q: A client wants more aerobic capacity but only does heavy lifting, because it feels hard. What does muscle plasticity imply?
o: Aerobic capacity is fixed, so nothing will change it
The stimulus decides what is built, so match the goal
Any hard training builds aerobic capacity equally
Heavy lifting builds more mitochondria than endurance work
e: Endurance work builds mitochondrial protein, so the muscle gains aerobic capacity. Resistance work builds contractile protein. Training has to match the goal rather than merely being hard.

q: A 50-year-old client has an estimated maximum heart rate of 173 and a resting rate of 70. What is a 60 to 75% heart rate reserve zone?
o: About 132 to 147 bpm
About 104 to 130 bpm
About 150 to 165 bpm
About 62 to 77 bpm
e: The reserve is 173 minus 70, which is 103. Target is resting rate plus the percentage of the reserve: 70 + 62 to 70 + 77. Taking 60 to 75% of the maximum instead gives 104 to 130, the cruder method.

q: A fit 45-year-old says the heart-rate zone you set from an age formula feels far too easy. What do you do?
o: Lower the zone, since feeling easy means they are overreaching
Treat it as a starting guess and adjust to how it feels
Switch them to 70% of maximum, which accounts for fitness
Keep the zone, since the formula is accurate for most people
e: Age formulas are off by about 10 to 12 beats either way for a typical person, and more for some. Treat zones built on them as a starting guess and check them against how hard it feels.

q: In the ACSM tables, what is the clearest difference between training for strength and for muscular endurance?
o: Frequency: strength is trained less often than endurance
Rest: 2 to 3 minutes for strength, 1 minute for endurance
Load: endurance uses 60 to 70% of 1RM, strength 30 to 50%
Sets: strength uses a single set, endurance several
e: Rest is the clearest difference, because longer rests let later sets stay heavy. Frequency rises the same way for both goals; the goal changes load, reps and rest.

q: A 68-year-old woman with low bone mass has trained at 60 to 70% of 1RM for months with good technique. She asks whether heavier lifting is off-limits. What do you say?
o: Switch to walking only, which protects bone best
Stay at 60 to 70% for good, as that is the ACSM ceiling
It has been shown safe when supervised, so progress it
Lift heavy only once a scan shows her bone has improved
e: The ACSM novice figure of 60 to 70% of 1RM is a start, not a ceiling. Supervised heavy lifting has been shown to be safe even in older women with low bone mass (fairly well supported).

q: Why do beginners gain strength quickly in their first weeks of lifting?
o: Tendons thicken before any change in the muscle
Muscle size roughly doubles within the first month
Mostly the nervous system learning the lift
Fat loss makes the same muscle appear stronger
e: Early strength gains are mostly neural: better fibre recruitment, coordination and motor learning (fairly well supported). Hypertrophy starts within weeks too but adds strength more slowly.

q: After two months a client's fast strength gains are slowing and they fear the programme has stopped working. What should you have told them at the start?
o: A slowdown means it is time to change programme entirely
Strength should keep rising at the same rate for a year
Gains slow because muscle has stopped growing altogether
That fast early gains always slow, so a slowdown is expected
e: The fast gains of the first couple of months always slow down. Say so in advance, so the slowdown reads as expected rather than as failure.

q: Once training volume is matched, how do periodised programmes compare with non-periodised ones?
o: Non-periodised programmes build clearly more muscle
Periodisation is required for any progress past a year
Any advantage is small or unproven
Periodised programmes roughly double strength gains
e: Periodised programmes have not been shown to beat non-periodised ones once volume is matched; at most a small extra gain in 1RM strength and none for muscle size. The structure is still useful for staying organised.

q: A client wants to add a little weight every week, indefinitely, and resists any lighter weeks. What is the best framing?
o: Lighter weeks are proven to double long-term results
Planned steps back make the next steps forward possible
Weekly increases can continue forever with good technique
Lighter weeks are only for competitive athletes near a peak
e: A periodised plan can rise like a sawtooth, each cycle starting below the last peak and climbing past it. Planned lighter weeks are sensible, though there is little evidence they improve results.

t: What is lost when someone stops
q: A client returns after two months off and feels surprisingly good in the first weeks back. Why?
o: Mitochondria are kept for years after stopping
Two months is too short to lose any adaptation
Plasma volume comes back quickly
Type II fibres grow during rest and recovery
e: What is gained fastest also disappears fastest, and comes back first. Plasma volume, and stroke volume with it, returns quickly, which is why the first weeks back feel better than they should.

t: What is lost when someone stops
q: Which adaptation is lost fastest when training stops?
o: Left ventricular mass
Capillaries
Mitochondria
Type I fibre size
e: Mitochondria, plasma volume and Type II fibre size go fastest. Left ventricular mass, cardiac contractile protein, Type I fibre size and capillaries are lost slowly.

q: When does delayed onset muscle soreness usually start and peak?
o: Starts during the session, peaks within an hour
Starts within 6 hours, gone by 24 hours
Starts after 3 days, peaks at about a week
Starts at 12 to 24 hours, peaks at 24 to 72
e: DOMS usually starts 12 to 24 hours after the session and peaks at 24 to 72 hours. The cause is eccentric muscle damage.

q: Two days after a hard first session, a client reports soreness far worse than usual, weak legs and dark, tea-coloured urine. What do you do?
o: Advise fluids and a light session to ease it
Wait a day to see whether it settles first
Reassure them it is normal DOMS and rest two days
Send them to A&E now as possible rhabdomyolysis
e: Soreness far worse than usual with weakness, swelling or dark urine may be rhabdomyolysis. Send the client to A&E and do not wait to see if it settles.

q: A client with constipation asks what they should change. Which two levers are within a trainer's scope?
o: A laxative supplement and a meal plan
Cutting out dairy and gluten for a month
A high-fibre elimination diet and a probiotic
More physical activity and more fluid
e: Physical activity speeds food through the gut. Activity and fluid are the two levers within a trainer's scope for constipation; anything beyond them is a referral.

q: What does bile do in digestion?
o: Breaks fat into droplets, a mechanical job
Acts as an acid that breaks down protein
Digests fat as an enzyme made in the gall bladder
Neutralises stomach acid as it leaves the stomach
e: Bile is neither an enzyme nor an acid; it breaks fat into droplets so pancreatic lipase can digest it. The gall bladder stores bile, and pancreatic bicarbonate neutralises stomach acid.

q: During a nutrition chat, a client mentions a change in bowel habit for the past four weeks and some weight loss they cannot explain. What do you do?
o: Start a food diary to find the trigger food
Refer them to their GP rather than change the diet
Suggest more fibre and fluid, then review in a month
Recommend a gut-health probiotic and more activity
e: Blood in the stool, a change in bowel habit lasting three weeks or more, unexplained weight loss or worsening abdominal pain mean referral to the GP, not a diet change.

q: Why do whole almonds deliver around 20% fewer calories than their label says?
o: Labels count the shell as well as the nut
Almond fat is a type the body cannot digest
Intact cell walls trap fat that is never absorbed
Chewing almonds burns off the missing calories
e: Chewing never breaks all the cell walls, so some fat is never absorbed. Grinding nuts into butter breaks the walls open and makes the fat available.

q: A client avoids fruit because it is simple sugar and eats white bread because it is a complex carbohydrate. What is accurate?
o: Fruit is fine only when it is blended into a smoothie
White bread raises glucose more than most fruit
Both raise blood glucose identically, as sugar is sugar
Correct: complex carbohydrate always raises glucose less
e: The evidence is against simple against complex as a health distinction. The useful axis is fibre, processing and food structure.

q: A client believes a calorie deficit means being hungry all the time. What approach best answers this?
o: Lower the energy density of their meals
Replace meals with low-calorie shakes
Eat smaller portions of the same meals
Cut out one meal a day entirely
e: Water and fibre lower energy density: vegetables, fruit, lean protein, pulses, anything bulky and not very fatty. It changes what is on the plate rather than how much.

q: What lowers a food's energy density?
o: Cooking it for longer
Fat and sugar
Salt and spices
Water and fibre
e: Energy density is calories per weight of food. Water and fibre add weight and bulk without many calories.

q: Why are drinks the best single target when cutting calories?
o: People do not eat less later to make up for them
Drinks are always denser in calories than solid food
Liquid sugar is stored as fat faster than solid food
Drinks raise appetite hormones for the rest of the day
e: Liquids satisfy hunger weakly, so 300 kcal in a drink is close to 300 kcal added, while 300 kcal of food usually displaces some of the next meal. An orange is about 45 kcal; an orange smoothie can be 500.

q: A client asks whether switching full-sugar cola for diet cola is worth it, having read that WHO advises against sweeteners. What is accurate?
o: It is pointless, since sweeteners cause the same weight gain
It only helps if they also stop eating sugar in food
It is harmful, as WHO found sweeteners raise weight in trials
Yes: trials support a modest benefit from the switch
e: Trials support a modest weight benefit from the switch. The 2023 WHO advice rests largely on observational data, which is prone to reverse causation: people already gaining weight are the ones who switch.

q: For a client in the UK, which national food guide should you use?
o: The DGE recommendations
The Harvard Healthy Eating Pyramid
MyPlate
The Eatwell Guide
e: Use the Eatwell Guide in the UK and the German Nutrition Society (DGE) recommendations in Germany. The January 2026 US guidelines replaced MyPlate with an inverted pyramid.

q: Which Harvard Healthy Eating Pyramid recommendation has not held up?
o: A daily multivitamin for healthy adults
Separating whole grains from refined grains
Treating plant oils as a base food
Keeping red meat apart from other proteins
e: Large trials have not found a daily multivitamin to help healthy adults who eat adequately. The other three changes, plus daily activity at the base, have held up.

q: Which four parts make up total daily energy expenditure?
o: RMR, EPOC, NEAT and TEF
RMR, TEF, EPOC and VO2
BMR, EAT, EPOC and RER
RMR, TEF, NEAT and EAT
e: Resting metabolic rate, the thermic effect of food, non-exercise activity thermogenesis and exercise activity thermogenesis. NASM's simpler version merges NEAT and EAT into physical activity.

q: Why is resting metabolism a smaller share of daily expenditure in an active person than in a sedentary one?
o: Resting metabolism stays fixed while the total grows
Active people digest their food much less efficiently
Exercise lowers resting metabolic rate over time
The thermic effect of food rises to about 30%
e: RMR is roughly fixed in calories, so when activity rises the resting share falls, from 60 to 75% to 40 to 60%. TEF stays at about 10% because it scales with intake.

q: A client wants to build muscle mainly to raise their metabolism for fat loss. What is accurate?
o: Greatly: muscle burns more per kilo than the heart
Only slightly: each kilo of muscle burns about 13 kcal a day
Greatly: each kilo of muscle burns about 100 kcal a day
Not at all: muscle adds nothing to resting metabolism
e: Muscle beats fat comfortably and loses heavily to every organ. Build it for strength, function and glucose control; the gain in metabolic rate is small.

q: Which component of daily energy expenditure is the largest lever available?
o: The thermic effect of food (TEF)
Everyday movement (NEAT)
Resting metabolic rate (RMR)
Structured exercise (EAT)
e: NEAT differs between people by hundreds of calories a day. RMR is the largest component but the least modifiable; TEF effects are real and small.

q: A client eating 500 kcal a day under their starting maintenance lost about a pound a week at first. After three months the loss has slowed. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Their body has stopped burning fat for fuel
Starvation mode has made further fat loss impossible
Maintenance has fallen, and intake may have crept up
They must be misreporting what they eat each day
e: A smaller body costs less to run and move, so the same intake gives a smaller deficit. Neither cause means they failed: re-measure, re-estimate and adjust.

q: As a rule of thumb, how far does a lasting change of 10 kcal a day eventually shift weight?
o: About one pound every month or so
About one pound every single week
About one kilogram each year, indefinitely
About one pound, over about three years
e: Half of the change happens in the first year and the full change takes about three years. The 3,500 kcal rule fails beyond the first few weeks because it assumes a body that does not change.

q: A client in a deficit says they feel sluggish and think they lack discipline. What is the accurate framing and action?
o: Their body is cutting everyday movement; schedule walks
Sluggishness means the deficit is working, so push on
They are short of caffeine, so add a pre-workout
They need more willpower, so add a daily motivation check
e: Much of adaptive thermogenesis is lost NEAT, which clients feel as tiredness rather than moving less. "Just move more" does not survive a diet; a scheduled walk does.

q: Which hormone drives hunger, and where is it made?
o: Ghrelin, from fat tissue
Ghrelin, from the stomach
Leptin, from fat tissue
Leptin, from the stomach
e: Ghrelin rises before meals and falls after eating. Leptin comes from fat tissue and signals fullness.

q: A client's eating goes wrong most on days after short nights. What is the likely link?
o: Short sleep raises metabolic rate, so they need more food
Short sleep probably raises ghrelin and lowers leptin
Short sleep lowers ghrelin and raises leptin
There is no known link between sleep and appetite
e: Short sleep probably raises the hunger hormone and lowers the fullness one, though the mechanism is likely rather than settled. That is why 7 to 9 hours of sleep is a weight-management variable.

q: A recreational athlete who under-eats around training asks which supplements to buy first. What is the best answer?
o: Buy a multivitamin to cover the gaps in their diet
Fix energy availability first, supplements last
Start with creatine and caffeine, then look at food
Start with a protein powder and a pre-workout
e: The hierarchy builds from energy availability, then macronutrients, micronutrients and timing. Supplements come last, once the four below are solid. People tend to build it upside down.

q: For endurance work and long sessions, what is the number one ergogenic aid?
o: Caffeine
Beta-alanine
Carbohydrate
Creatine
e: Carbohydrate comes ahead of every supplement for long sessions (well supported). For short strength sessions, creatine and caffeine have the better evidence.

q: A client training hard has repeated niggling injuries, poor recovery and flat motivation. What belongs on your list of causes?
o: Poor motivation, which leads to careless technique
Weak core stability, which causes most niggling injuries
Food intake, alongside programming and sleep
Programming alone, since injuries are a load problem
e: Chronic under-fuelling relative to training shows up as an injury and recovery problem, not as a nutrition problem. The common pattern is under-fuelling around training, then eating a lot later.

q: A client answers yes to two questions on the SCOFF questionnaire. What do you do?
o: Refer only at three or more yes answers
Refer them on
Set them a structured meal plan
Monitor them for another month
e: SCOFF is a five-question screen for eating disorders; two or more yes answers mean refer on.

q: A client added five sessions a week, changed nothing else, and has lost far less than their calories burned predicted. What is accurate?
o: Exercise has slowed their metabolism down permanently
They must be under-reporting how much food they eat
The body compensates, with more appetite and less movement
Their sessions are not intense enough to burn any fat
e: Exercise alone produces modest weight loss (fairly well supported). A session burns little next to a day's spending, and the body partly makes up for it. That is physiology, not a lack of willpower.

q: A client starting semaglutide asks what their training should focus on. What is the best answer?
o: Stretching and mobility, as appetite will be low
Very light training until the dose is stable
High-volume cardio to add to the weight loss
Resistance training and enough protein
e: Clients on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs lose a lot of lean tissue, often around a third of the weight lost. Low appetite can make protein and fluid the problem.

q: A client wants to drop to a very low intake to shock their fat loss. What is the likely result?
o: A complete metabolic shutdown within the first week
Faster, lasting fat loss with no change in metabolism
More muscle gain, driven by the stress response
Expenditure is turned down, starting with movement
e: Cut intake far enough and expenditure is turned down to match, which is why aggressive restriction so often stalls. The first thing cut is usually everyday movement.

q: What happens to the stress response as intake falls sharply?
o: It rises, with cortisol, against the goal
It rises, which speeds up fat loss
It is unaffected by how much someone eats
It falls, which helps release stored fat
e: The stress response rises as intake falls, cortisol with it, and that works against the goal rather than for it.

q: Six weeks into lifting, a client's strength is up and their waist is smaller, but the scale has not moved. What is the best response?
o: Stop lifting, since the new muscle hides fat loss
Cut calories further until the scale starts to move
Add daily cardio to force the scale weight down
Judge progress by strength and body composition
e: Some people build muscle faster than they lose fat, so the scale stalls while body composition improves. Health markers can improve without much change on the scale.

q: A client wearing a glucose monitor wants to eliminate every rise in blood sugar after meals. What is accurate?
o: Every rise after a meal damages metabolic health
They should cut all carbohydrate to flatten the curve
Rises are normal; removing them is not a health goal
Rises only matter if they happen after breakfast
e: Blood sugar rising and falling after meals is normal. Treating every rise as a problem pushes people towards needless restriction.

q: A client breaks an ankle and plans to cut calories hard because training has stopped. What do you advise?
o: Eat around maintenance and keep protein high
Cut hard, since the missed training has lowered their needs
Eat well above maintenance to speed healing
Fast for a few days to reduce inflammation
e: Metabolic rate goes up during healing, and walking on crutches costs two to three times normal walking. Cutting hard delays return and prevents full healing.

q: By roughly how much does healing raise energy expenditure?
o: About 100 to 200%
About 1 to 5%
About 15 to 50%
It falls by about 20%
e: Healing raises expenditure by roughly 15 to 50%, depending on how serious the injury is, so needs fall much less than the lost training suggests.

q: In a calorie deficit without resistance training, roughly what share of the weight lost is often lean tissue?
o: Almost none
About a quarter
About half
About three quarters
e: Often around a quarter without resistance training, and the leaner the person, the bigger that share. Lifting and enough protein shrink it.

q: During exercise insulin is suppressed. How does working muscle still take up glucose?
o: Adrenaline carries glucose into the muscle fibres
It has a second uptake route that runs only during exercise
The brain releases glucose directly into the muscle
It cannot, so it runs on fat alone until insulin returns
e: Normally muscle and liver need insulin to take up glucose. Working muscle has a second way in, but loses insulin's protection against breakdown exactly when it is under load.

t: Gaining muscle and losing fat at once
q: An untrained new client carrying excess fat asks whether they can build muscle while losing fat. What is the best answer?
o: Yes: clients like this are likeliest to manage it
Only in advanced lifters who know their maintenance
No: it is impossible, so bulk first and cut later
Only with a calorie surplus of 500 kcal or more
e: It is most achievable in people who are untrained, detrained or carrying excess fat, which describes most new clients. The further from their ceiling, the more room to do both.

t: Gaining muscle and losing fat at once
q: Which client has the least room to gain muscle and lose fat at the same time?
o: A lean, highly trained lifter near their ceiling
A novice in their first year of lifting
A detrained former athlete returning to the gym
An untrained beginner who carries excess fat
e: The further someone is from their ceiling, the more room there is to do both at once.

q: For a client lifting to build or keep muscle, around what daily protein intake do the gains level off?
o: About 0.8 g/kg
About 1.6 g/kg
About 3.0 g/kg
About 1.0 g/kg
e: Gains level off around 1.6 g/kg (Morton 2018; well supported); the ISSN gives 1.5 to 2.0. 0.8 g/kg is the sedentary RDA, enough for health but not training.

q: A 130 kg client carrying a lot of body fat is starting a deficit. How should you set their protein target?
o: 0.8 g/kg of their current body weight
2.0 to 2.4 g/kg of their current body weight
1.6 g/kg of their current body weight
1.2 to 1.6 g/kg of adjusted or target weight
e: For a client carrying a lot of fat, base the target on adjusted or target weight, not current weight. 2.0 to 2.4 g/kg is for lean, trained people in a deficit.

q: A client eats almost no protein until dinner, then has 120 g in one meal. What is the best advice?
o: Cut the total, since 120 g at once strains the kidneys
Most of the dinner protein is wasted beyond about 0.4 g/kg
Keep the total and move some protein earlier in the day
Nothing, since the timing of protein never matters
e: Total daily protein matters most. The hard per-serving ceiling is no longer well supported, but someone eating all their protein at dinner spends most of the day below the leucine trigger.

q: A healthy client worries that a high protein intake will damage their kidneys. What is accurate?
o: They should have their kidneys tested before 1.6 g/kg
The evidence is against harm to healthy kidneys
Protein above 1.2 g/kg damages the kidneys over time
High protein is safe only if it comes from plants
e: Clearing urea takes work and water, but for healthy kidneys and liver that is routine. Kidney disease is a medical question and a referral.

q: A 72-year-old client exercises three times a week. What is their minimum daily protein target on the PROT-AGE recommendations?
o: At least 2.0 g/kg
At least 1.0 g/kg
At least 0.8 g/kg
At least 1.2 g/kg
e: PROT-AGE gives at least 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg for adults over 65, at least 1.2 if they exercise, and 1.2 to 1.5 with acute or chronic illness.

q: Why do collagen supplements not count towards a muscle-building protein target?
o: It lacks tryptophan, an essential amino acid
It is absorbed only into the skin and the joints
It contains no leucine of any kind
It is a plant protein with a limiting amino acid
e: Nearly all animal proteins carry all nine essential amino acids. Collagen and gelatin are the exception, lacking tryptophan.

q: NASM's table lists methionine as the missing amino acid in legumes. What is accurate?
o: Methionine is entirely absent from all legumes
Lysine, not methionine, is absent from legumes
Legumes contain no essential amino acids
Methionine is present, but in a limiting amount
e: Plant proteins almost always contain all nine essential amino acids; one is present in a lower amount. The difference is between a shortfall you can top up and an absence you cannot.

q: A vegan client has been told they must combine beans and grains in the same meal to get complete protein. What is accurate?
o: Combining foods makes no difference to plant protein
They must be eaten within an hour of each other
Correct: they must be eaten within the same meal
Covering the profile across the day is enough
e: The old advice that complementary foods had to be eaten together was wrong, and the correction is well established.

q: A vegan client asks whether they need more protein than an omnivore. What is the accurate answer?
o: The same total, but a bigger serving per meal
The same total and the same size of serving
Less, since plant protein is absorbed better
About twice the daily total an omnivore needs
e: Total requirements are roughly the same. Per meal, plant proteins carry less leucine, so a bigger serving is needed; once it clears the threshold, the result is the same.

q: A lacto-ovo-vegetarian lifter eats about 1.04 g/kg of protein a day. What is the priority?
o: Nothing, since 1.04 g/kg is above the RDA
Switch to animal protein to build muscle
Pair legumes and grains at every meal
Raise the total towards about 1.6 g/kg
e: The average vegetarian intake is about two thirds of what training asks for. Eggs and dairy are complete and rich in leucine, so what remains is hitting the total.

q: A client going fully vegan asks which supplement is essential. What do you tell them?
o: Iron
Protein powder
Creatine
Vitamin B12
e: B12 is essentially absent from plant foods, and deficiency causes irreversible nerve damage. It is essential to supplement on a vegan diet.

q: A vegetarian client relies on plant sources of iron. What practical advice helps absorption?
o: Eat iron-rich foods with dairy to aid absorption
Nothing: plant iron is absorbed as well as meat iron
Pair them with vitamin C, away from tea and coffee
Take iron with coffee, since caffeine speeds uptake
e: Non-haem iron from plants is absorbed far less well than haem iron, and phytates, tea and coffee reduce it further. Vitamin C improves uptake a lot.

q: A client who is cutting wants to switch to light, high-rep circuits to tone up while dieting. What do you advise?
o: Stop lifting until the diet is finished
Keep the volume and reduce the load to recover
Switch to circuits, since high reps burn more fat
Hold the load, and cut the volume instead
e: Load is the signal that keeps muscle. Dropping volume in a deficit is fine; dropping intensity is what costs tissue. Switching to circuits is probably the commonest error.

q: A lean client at about 10% body fat wants to cut. What rate of loss do you aim for?
o: The top of the range, to finish the cut quickly
About 2% of bodyweight every week
Whatever a 1,000 kcal daily deficit gives
The bottom of the 0.5 to 1% a week range
e: As body fat falls, a greater share of any deficit comes from lean tissue. Someone at 30% body fat can take the top of the range; someone at 10% should not.

q: A client eats a large, high-fat, high-fibre meal half an hour before training and feels heavy. What do you suggest?
o: Quick-to-digest carbohydrate, low in fat and fibre
A bigger meal with more protein to fuel the session
A high-fibre snack instead, for slower energy
Training fasted from now on to avoid discomfort
e: Before training, choose carbohydrate that is quick to digest, scaled to the time available and how hard the session will be. Fat, fibre and protein slow the emptying of the stomach, which you do not want when training starts.

q: When does a client need to take on fuel during a session?
o: Only once sessions run past about 45 minutes
Only in resistance sessions, never in cardio
Only in sessions that last over three hours
In every session, to keep blood glucose stable
e: Fuelling during exercise is only needed once sessions run long. Below about three quarters of an hour, water.

q: A runner gets stomach trouble when they take gels in races. What is the best approach?
o: Switch to solid food, which the gut handles better
Avoid all fuel in races to protect their gut from it
Practise gels only in the one long run each week
Practise on ordinary training days, starting small
e: Gut trouble during exercise is largely trainable (fairly well supported). Start small, build slowly, and practise the race-day plan on ordinary training days, not only on the one long session a week.

q: A cyclist switches to honey as a natural fuel and develops gut symptoms. What is the likely cause?
o: Honey digests too slowly
Honey contains lactose
Honey is high in fructose
Honey raises stomach acid
e: Fructose, like lactose, draws water into the gut when undigested, and honey is high in it. Also check caffeine, dehydration and competition stress before blaming the food.

q: A client had two glasses of wine after training and asks whether they undid the session. What is accurate?
o: No: the effect depends on dose, and is far smaller at two
No: alcohol has no effect on recovery at any dose
Yes: wine blocks protein synthesis more than beer
Yes: any alcohol within 24 hours cancels the session
e: The headline study, Parr 2014, used about 1.5 g/kg, eight or nine drinks for an average man. Moderate intake has a much smaller effect.

q: Why does the day after drinking often go wrong for eating?
o: Alcohol raises next-day metabolic rate, so hunger follows
The liver stops using fat for two days
Alcohol has no calories, so the body demands more
Disrupted sleep shifts the hunger hormones
e: Alcohol may ease falling asleep but disrupts sleep later in the night and reduces REM. Poor sleep shifts the hunger and fullness hormones the next day. Alcohol provides 7 calories per gram.

q: Which describes a food allergy rather than an intolerance?
o: An immune response, possibly life-threatening
A reaction that often fades as the diet changes
Bloating and wind that depend on how much is eaten
Symptoms that change with stress and gut health
e: A food allergy is an immune system response, needs a formal medical diagnosis and strict avoidance. Intolerance is dose-dependent digestive symptoms.

q: A client says they are allergic to dairy because it bloats them. What is the best way to think about it?
o: Treat it as a severe allergy and ban all dairy for good
Bloating fits intolerance; allergy needs a medical diagnosis
Test it by giving them some dairy during a session
Tell them it is only intolerance, so eat dairy freely
e: Misidentifying an intolerance as an allergy leads to fear and restriction; treating an allergy as a minor intolerance can be dangerous. Allergy needs a formal medical diagnosis.

q: A client with bloating wants to cut out gluten and dairy. What should come first?
o: A strict elimination diet of both foods for a month
Portion size, meal timing, fibre type and hydration
A gluten-free diet first, then dairy if needed
A probiotic and a digestive enzyme supplement
e: These levers are a better answer than cutting foods out (fairly well supported), and they sit within a trainer's scope in a way an elimination diet does not.

q: A client eats lunch in five minutes at their desk and complains of indigestion. What is accurate?
o: Eating fast or distracted impairs digestion
Speed does not matter if the food itself is healthy
Only the food itself can cause indigestion
It points to a food intolerance that needs finding
e: Symptoms are shaped by stress, sleep, hydration, activity, eating speed, meal timing and gut movement, not by food alone.

q: A client says they are on keto: 60% of calories from fat and about 100 g of carbohydrate a day. Is it ketogenic?
o: Yes: 100 g of carbohydrate is low enough
No: keto is defined by carbohydrate, not fat
Only if protein is also below 10%
Yes: any diet above 60% fat is ketogenic
e: The defining feature is carbohydrate restriction; high fat is the result. Count the grams of carbohydrate, not the fat percentage.

q: Which dietary pattern has the best evidence, on trial data as well as observation?
o: Vegan
Carnivore
Mediterranean
Ketogenic
e: The Mediterranean pattern is the best-evidenced (fairly well supported). PREDIMED was re-analysed in 2018 after randomisation problems, and the result held.

q: A client asks whether low-carb or low-fat is better for weight loss. What is the accurate answer?
o: Low-carb wins, because it keeps insulin lower
It depends on their genes, which a test can show
Matched for calories and protein, they are nearly equal
Low-fat wins, because fat has more calories per gram
e: Calories and protein are the dials (well supported). Everything else is preference, adherence and context.

q: Why does intermittent fasting help some people lose weight?
o: Eating late at night is stored as fat
Fasting raises metabolic rate for the whole day
A shorter eating window makes eating less easier
Fasting switches on a special fat-burning state
e: Nothing metabolically special is happening. As with any elimination diet, it works by reducing calories; the timing is not doing the work.

q: A client's diet gets steadily cleaner while their life gets smaller; they now skip social events to avoid food. What do you recognise?
o: A warning sign dressed up as compliance
A sign they are ready for a stricter plan
Excellent adherence that deserves praise
A normal phase that passes after a few weeks
e: At the extreme, calling foods virtuous or evil becomes orthorexia. It is the version a trainer is most likely to meet, because it looks like compliance.

q: What decides whether a diet works for a given client?
o: Whether it is backed by the most research
How strictly the rules are written
The client's willpower and character
Whether it is achievable for them
e: A diet should be safe, effective, healthy and achievable; achievable decides the outcome. The design of the plan, not the character of the person, decides adherence.

q: A client panics because they missed the 30-minute window after lifting. What is accurate?
o: Only carbohydrate needs to arrive within 30 minutes
The session was wasted without protein in 30 minutes
The 30-minute rule is not supported; totals matter more
They should double their protein at the next meal
e: Muscles are more sensitive to nutrients for about two hours, and the effect fades gradually. A 30 g shake straight after is fine; so is chicken an hour later.

q: Which client genuinely benefits from fast carbohydrate straight after training?
o: A gym-goer doing three full-body sessions a week
A client lifting each muscle group twice a week
A runner training the same muscles daily
Anyone who has just finished resistance training
e: Resistance training moderately depletes glycogen, and ordinary meals restore it before the next session. For people training the same muscles on consecutive days, a 2-hour delay cuts replenishment by about 50%.

q: What is the dose for creatine monohydrate?
o: 20 g a day, every day, to stay loaded
1 g a day, taken only before training
5 g taken within 30 minutes of each session
5 g a day, or 20 g a day for a week
e: 5 g a day from a standing start, or 20 g a day for a week to load faster. It needs consistency and does not care when it is taken.

q: A client's pre-workout contains 2 g of beta-alanine, taken only on training days. Will it help?
o: No: it needs larger daily doses for four weeks
No: beta-alanine has no evidence at any dose
Yes, but only for efforts under 10 seconds
Yes: 2 g before each session is the effective dose
e: The studies used 4 to 6.4 g a day in divided doses, daily for 4 weeks, against 1.8 to 3.2 g in products. A dose inside a pre-workout does nothing unless taken daily regardless of training.

q: A pregnant client asks how much caffeine she can have. What is the EFSA limit?
o: No more than 100 mg a day
None at all during pregnancy
No more than 400 mg a day
No more than 200 mg a day
e: Up to 400 mg a day is safe for healthy adults, with single doses up to 200 mg, and no more than 200 mg a day in pregnancy.

q: A client wants to use caffeine to improve performance. What dose and timing does the evidence use?
o: 3 to 6 mg/kg about an hour before
3 to 6 mg/kg straight after the session
1 mg/kg just before the session starts
10 mg/kg two hours before training
e: Caffeine is well supported as a performance aid, about 2% for endurance. Habitual users need the top of the range. To protect sleep, a pre-workout should be at least 13 hours before bed.

q: In what order does the assessment run?
o: Posture, body measures, paper, then movement
Movement, paper, posture, then body measures
Body measures, movement, posture, then paper
Paper, posture, movement, then body and heart
e: First establish who the person is and whether it is safe to train them. Each step narrows what the next one looks for.

q: A keen new client wants to start with a fitness test straight away. What must come first?
o: A body-fat measurement, to set the outcome goal
Establishing who they are and that it is safe
A maximal test, to set the most accurate baseline
An overhead squat, to find their overactive muscles
e: The assessment starts on paper: the PAR-Q+ and lifestyle questionnaire establish safety and context before posture, movement and measurement.

q: A client answers yes to one of the seven PAR-Q+ general questions. What happens next?
o: The trainer decides on the spot whether to go ahead
They are barred from exercise until a doctor clears them
They sign the declaration and start as normal
Follow-up pages, which can lead to clearance or referral
e: All no answers clear the client to become more active. Any yes leads to follow-up pages on chronic conditions, which can require medical clearance or referral.

q: Why ask a new client whether a close relative died suddenly of a heart problem under the age of 50?
o: It predicts how fast they gain fitness
It is needed for their heart rate zone
It decides whether they may lift heavy
It flags inherited heart conditions
e: Inherited heart conditions cause most exercise-related deaths in young people. The ACSM screening also asks whether the person exercises now, whether they have known heart, metabolic or kidney disease or symptoms, and how hard they want to train.

q: At rest, a client's blood pressure reads 184/112. They feel fine, with no symptoms. What do you do?
o: No training until they have seen their doctor
Recheck after a warm-up and train if it drops
Train at a low intensity and recheck afterwards
Call emergency services at once, as it is a crisis
e: A resting reading of 180/110 or more means no training until the client has seen their doctor (ACSM). Call emergency services only above 180/120 with chest pain, severe headache, vision change, breathlessness or confusion.

q: A client on insulin checks their blood glucose before a session: 4.6 mmol/L. What happens?
o: You advise them to skip their next insulin dose
They eat carbohydrate first, with fast sugar to hand
They cancel the session and you send them to A&E
They train as normal, since the reading is in range
e: Below about 5 mmol/L before a session, a client on insulin or sulphonylureas eats carbohydrate first. The client and their diabetes team set the glucose plan, not the trainer; hypos can come hours later.

q: During a hard session in the heat, a client becomes confused and starts behaving strangely. What do you do?
o: Let them rest for 20 minutes to see if it passes
Drive them to hospital straight away before cooling
Sit them in the shade and give water, then reassess
Call an ambulance and cool them at once
e: Treat confusion, strange behaviour or collapse during hard exercise in the heat as heat stroke until proven otherwise. Cooling comes before transport.

q: Why should you avoid taking a client's pulse at the carotid artery in the neck?
o: The carotid pulse is too weak to count reliably at rest
Pressing the carotid sinus can drop heart rate and pressure
The carotid is too hard to find on most clients
The carotid pulse runs faster than the radial
e: Reaching for the neck also causes anxiety that raises the reading, and too much pressure can block blood flow to the brain. The baroreceptor reflex may cause dizziness or fainting, especially in older adults. Use the radial pulse.

q: How fast should you deflate the cuff when taking blood pressure?
o: In one quick release
About 2 to 3 mmHg per second
About 5 to 10 mmHg per second
About 1 mmHg every 5 seconds
e: Inflate until the radial pulse disappears, then at least 30 mmHg higher, and deflate at 2 to 3 mmHg per second while listening.

q: A client arrives for a blood-pressure check straight after a double espresso and a brisk walk up the stairs. What do you do?
o: Measure straight away, then average with a later reading
Measure while they walk it off on the treadmill
Measure straight away and subtract 10 mmHg
Wait 30 minutes, then seat them quietly for five
e: No caffeine, exercise or smoking in the previous 30 minutes. The client sits for five minutes, back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level, without talking. Take two or three readings a minute apart.

q: Which method is the most accurate lab reference for body fat?
o: A DEXA scan alone
Bioelectrical impedance
Underwater weighing alone
A four-compartment model
e: The most accurate lab reference is a four-compartment model, which combines several measurements. Underwater weighing and DEXA are reference methods with their own error; underwater weighing assumes a fixed density for lean tissue.

q: A client's impedance scale shows their body fat up 3% overnight, after a hot day on which they drank little. What is the likely cause?
o: Skin temperature changes the reading, not fluid
They gained fat overnight from the heat
Impedance readings depend heavily on hydration
The reading is correct, since impedance is a reference method
e: Bioelectrical impedance gives a good indication, but depends heavily on hydration, so a dry day can shift the reading without any change in fat.

q: What is the commonest error when taking a skinfold measurement?
o: Reading the callipers within one to two seconds
Pinching only skin, not the fat beneath
Repeating a site until two readings agree
Waiting 15 seconds before repeating a site
e: Get a good grip and pull the fat away from the muscle, fingers 5 to 7 cm apart. Waiting 15 seconds, reading within two seconds and repeating a site are correct practice.

q: A muscular rugby player with a BMI of 29 has been told he is overweight. What is accurate?
o: Correct: a BMI of 29 always means excess body fat
BMI overestimates fat only in short people
BMI cannot tell muscle from fat in one person
BMI is accurate for athletes but not for older adults
e: BMI counts muscle, fat, bone and fluid the same, so it tracks body fat across a population and still misclassifies many individuals. Use it to understand risk, not to estimate one person's body composition.

q: A client is 170 cm tall with a waist of 90 cm. Which NICE waist-to-height band are they in?
o: High risk (0.6 or more)
Increased risk (0.5 to 0.59)
Healthy (0.4 to 0.49)
Healthy, since the waist is under 94 cm
e: 90 divided by 170 is about 0.53. NICE bands: 0.4 to 0.49 healthy, 0.5 to 0.59 increased risk, 0.6 or more high risk. The target is a waist under half the height.

q: A new client has a history of disordered eating. How do you handle body-composition measurement?
o: Take skinfolds as normal, but keep the results private
Use BMI only, since it is the least personal
Make it opt-in, including the option of nothing
Weigh them weekly so progress is clear
e: Make body-composition measurement opt-in, and offer tape, performance measures or nothing to anyone with a history of disordered eating.

q: How is the overhead squat assessment performed?
o: Ten reps, barefoot, arms folded, watched from behind
Five reps, barefoot, arms overhead, from front and side
Three reps, in shoes, hands on hips, watched from the front
One rep to full depth, arms by the sides, watched from the side
e: Feet shoulder-width apart and pointing straight ahead, arms overhead with elbows straight, squatting to thighs parallel with depth adjusted as needed.

q: During the overhead squat, a client's knees buckle in. Besides the hips, what should you check?
o: Shoulder mobility
Ankle dorsiflexion
Neck position
Lumbar extension
e: NASM reads knees buckling in as inner-thigh overactivity and outer-hip weakness, and also says to check ankle dorsiflexion, which is why raising the heels is the standard regression. Treat the reading as a hypothesis to test.

q: A colleague says the overhead squat shows which clients will go on to injure their ACL. What is accurate?
o: Knee valgus has not predicted ACL injury in large studies
It predicts injury only when seen on all five reps
It predicts ACL injury in women but not in men
Correct: knee valgus in a squat reliably predicts ACL injury
e: Knee valgus in a jump or squat has not predicted ACL injury in large studies that followed people forward in time (the evidence is against it). The squat helps find something to test; it does not forecast injury.

q: What should you compare a client's movement battery against?
o: An ideal posture chart from a standard textbook
Their own left and right, and their past results
The results of other clients training at the gym
Population norms for someone of their age and sex
e: Compare left with right, and today with last month, not with population norms: there is no agreed picture of good posture, and static posture predicts pain poorly. Know roughly how big a change has to be before it is real.

q: A gym manager wants to use the Functional Movement Screen to predict which members will get injured. What is accurate?
o: The FMS predicts injury only in athletes, not members
The FMS is accurate if two assessors agree on the score
Screens do not predict injury; use it for a baseline
The FMS predicts injury well in members over 40
e: The FMS and SFMA have repeatedly failed in systematic reviews, among them Moran 2017 and Bunn 2019. Assess to find asymmetries and to have a baseline you can re-measure.

q: Which Anatomy Trains line does dissection support poorly?
o: The superficial front line
The superficial back line
The functional lines
The spiral line
e: Wilke 2016 found good support for the superficial back and functional lines, moderate for the spiral and lateral lines, and poor for the superficial front line.

q: A colleague treats a client's calf complaint at the far end of a myofascial line, sure the force travels along it. What is accurate?
o: The lines are proven for the calf but not the shoulder
The lines suggest where to look, not proven force paths
Force does not pass between neighbouring muscles at all
Correct: force travels usefully along every line
e: Force does pass between neighbouring muscles (fairly well supported), but there is little evidence that clinically meaningful force travels along a whole line.

q: In what order should you run the assessment tests?
o: Any order, as long as all are done
Upper body first, then lower body
From least to most demanding
From most to least demanding
e: Ordering from least to most demanding means that if a client shows signs of being overwhelmed, you can stop and carry the rest over rather than losing the whole baseline.

q: Halfway through the battery, a nervous new client is visibly overwhelmed. What do you do?
o: Finish the battery quickly so the baseline is complete
Skip to the hardest test to get it out of the way
Stop and carry the rest over to another session
Push through, since stopping would undermine them
e: Completing the battery matters, but not more than the client coming back. Avoid tests that end in visible failure for a client who is already unsure about being there.

q: During a hard set, a client's blood pressure reads 256/100. What do you do?
o: Finish the set, then rest before the next one
Stop the session
Lower the load and carry on at a moderate effort
Carry on, since pressure rises normally during lifting
e: During a session, a systolic above 250 or a diastolic above 115 means stop the session. Pressure does rise with effort, but not that far.

q: In a graded test, a client's systolic pressure starts to fall as the workload rises. What does it mean for the session?
o: It is a sign of good fitness, so continue
Stop the session
Nothing, as long as diastolic stays under 115
Slow the increments and keep going
e: Systolic falling as the work rises is one of the in-session stop signs, alongside a systolic above 250 or a diastolic above 115.

q: At rest, a client's blood pressure reads 186/124 and they report a severe headache and blurred vision. What do you do?
o: Call emergency services
No training today; they book a GP appointment
Recheck in 10 minutes and train if it drops
Let them sit quietly, then do a light session
e: Above 180/120 with chest pain, severe headache, a change in vision, breathlessness or confusion, call emergency services (American Heart Association). Without symptoms, 180/110 or more means no training until they see their doctor.

q: A client with type 1 diabetes checks their blood glucose before a session: 15.5 mmol/L. What happens next?
o: They train as normal, since exercise will lower it
They eat carbohydrate first, with fast sugar to hand
They check ketones, and do not train if raised
You suggest they take extra insulin before starting
e: Above about 14 mmol/L before a session, a client with type 1 diabetes checks ketones and does not train if they are raised. The client and their diabetes team set the glucose plan, not the trainer.

q: A client with back pain mentions numbness around the groin and new trouble controlling their bladder. What do you do?
o: Suggest a GP appointment within the next few weeks
Avoid loaded spinal flexion and review next session
Switch to gentle mobility work until it eases
Treat it as an emergency: same-day medical help
e: Back pain with numbness around the groin, new bladder or bowel problems, or weakness in both legs is an emergency, same day. It is a red flag, not a programming question.

q: NICE (NG246) lowers the BMI thresholds for people of South Asian, Chinese, Black African or African-Caribbean origin. What are they?
o: 25 and 30, the same as everyone else
27 and 32
20 and 25
e: People of these origins carry higher cardiometabolic risk at a lower BMI, so NICE uses 23 and 27.5 for them in place of 25 and 30. More lean mass at a given BMI in Black adults does not make their risk lower.

q: A man's waist, measured midway between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone, is 98 cm. What do the waist cut-offs say?
o: Substantially increased risk, since it is over 94 cm
Increased risk: over 94 cm but not over 102 cm
Healthy, since the male cut-off is 102 cm
Healthy, since only waist-to-hip ratio counts
e: For men, over 94 cm is increased risk and over 102 cm substantially increased; for women the figures are 80 and 88 cm. The cut-offs assume the midway site, and are lower for Asian populations.

q: A client's feet roll in too far when they squat. In NASM's domino chain, what happens next, working up from the foot?
o: The thigh bone turns outwards and that hip lifts
The pelvis tilts forwards before the knee is affected
The shoulders round forwards before the hips change
The shin turns inwards too far, and the thigh follows
e: NASM's chain runs foot, shin, thigh, hip, then shoulders: excessive pronation turns the shin inwards and the thigh turns with it, and that hip drops. Pronation itself is normal; the chain describes too much of it.

q: A client has knee pain, and you notice their hip drops on that side. How should you use the idea of regional interdependence?
o: As proof that the hip is causing the knee pain
As irrelevant, since pain starts where it is felt
As a reason to keep training through pain that is not settling
As a reason to look beyond the knee, not as a diagnosis
e: Regional interdependence is fairly well supported: what presents at one site may originate at another. It is a reason to look, not a diagnosis, and pain that is not settling should be referred.

q: Which of these is one of the five functions of the skeleton?
o: Producing digestive hormones
Storing minerals
Producing heat to maintain homeostasis
Lubricating the joint surfaces
e: The five are shape and form, support and protection of organs, structure for movement, blood cell production and mineral storage. Heat comes from skeletal muscle, and lubrication from synovial fluid.

q: In an adult, where is red, blood-producing marrow found?
o: The shafts of the femur and humerus
The carpals and tarsals of the hands and feet
The pelvis, vertebrae, sternum and ribs
The skull and the patella only
e: Red marrow sits in the pelvis, vertebrae, sternum, ribs and the ends of the femur and humerus. The shaft of an adult long bone holds mostly yellow, fatty marrow.

q: Which division of the skeleton contains the skull, rib cage and vertebral column?
o: Appendicular, about 126 bones
Axial, about 80 bones
Axial, about 126 bones
Appendicular, about 80 bones
e: The axial skeleton has approximately 80 bones: skull, rib cage and vertebral column. The appendicular skeleton, approximately 126 bones, holds the arms, legs and pelvic girdle.

q: Which of these belongs to the appendicular skeleton?
o: The pelvic girdle
The rib cage
The vertebral column
The skull
e: The appendicular skeleton is the arms, legs and pelvic girdle. The pelvis is easy to misplace as axial because it sits at the base of the trunk.

q: A 70-year-old client walks daily and cycles twice a week to protect her bones. What should you add?
o: More walking, building up towards an hour a day
Progressive resistance work, including the upper body
Swimming, to load the whole skeleton evenly at once
Longer cycling sessions at a higher cadence
e: Walking, cycling and swimming are good for health but weak for bone, and do nothing for the wrists and arms. The wrist is what people land on when they fall, so an upper-body resistance component belongs in every older client's programme.

q: Bone is constantly remodelled. What do osteoclasts and osteoblasts each do?
o: Osteoblasts remove old bone; osteoclasts lay down new
Both lay down new bone, at different ages
Osteoclasts store minerals; osteoblasts make blood cells
Osteoclasts remove old bone; osteoblasts lay down new
e: Osteoclasts remove old bone and osteoblasts lay down new. The names are easy to swap; one way to hold it is that osteoblasts build.

q: What makes the patella a sesamoid bone?
o: It is flat and protects the joint beneath it
It is irregular in shape, like a vertebra
It sits in a tendon where it crosses a joint
It is short and cube-like, like the carpals
e: Sesamoid bones are small bones embedded in a tendon where it crosses a joint. The patella, in the quadriceps tendon, is the largest.

q: The vertebrae and the sacrum are classed as which type of bone?
o: Irregular
Flat
Short
Long
e: Vertebrae and the sacrum are irregular bones. The sternum is the example of a flat bone and the carpals of a short one.

q: At roughly what age does bone mass peak?
o: About 18, when growth stops
Late twenties to around 30
Around 40, just before midlife
Around 50, at the menopause
e: Most bone mass is laid down by about 18 to 20, but it peaks in the late twenties to around 30, holds until midlife and then declines. The tempting answer of 18 confuses 'mostly laid down' with the peak.

q: Which two periods of life are the windows where loading bone matters most?
o: Adolescence and the menopause transition
Early childhood and the late twenties
The late twenties and the start of midlife
Midlife and the eighties
e: Adolescence is when most bone mass is laid down, and loss is fastest in women in the first years after menopause. Those are the two windows where loading matters most.

q: You want to check a client's pelvic tilt from the front. Where do you put your thumbs to find the ASIS?
o: Thumbs under the two dimples either side of the base of the spine
