Fingers along the top edge of the pelvis, where the hands rest
Hands on hips, thumbs forward, on the bony point at the front
Thumbs on the outside of the upper thigh, below the iliac crest
e: The ASIS is the bony point at the front with hands on hips and thumbs forward. The dimples mark the PSIS, the top edge is the iliac crest, and the outer thigh is the greater trochanter.

q: Standing, a client rolls their feet inwards and sees their knees and hips move too. Which idea does this show?
o: Arthrokinematics: surfaces sliding inside one joint
The all-or-nothing principle of muscle activation
The kinetic chain: linked joints move together
Open chain movement of the distal segments
e: The kinetic chain is the linked joints and muscles that move together, so moving one joint moves the others. The feet are fixed on the floor here, so it is not open chain.

q: Besides letting bones move, what else do joints do?
o: Produce the force that moves the bones
Stop bones moving in ways they should not
Store the minerals the bones need
Pull the bones back into place after each movement
e: Joints let bones move and also stop them moving in ways they should not. Force comes from muscles, which can only pull, and minerals are stored in bone.

q: Approximately what proportion of the body's joints are synovial?
o: 20 per cent
50 per cent
80 per cent
95 per cent
e: Synovial joints make up about 80 per cent of the body's joints, have the greatest capacity for motion and predominate in the limbs.

q: What does synovial fluid do?
o: Lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage
Connects the bones to one another inside the capsule
Forms the cartilage that lines the ends of the bones
Absorbs shock between the vertebrae of the spine
e: Secreted by the synovial membrane, the fluid lubricates the joint surfaces, reducing wear, and nourishes the cartilage cells. Shock absorption between vertebrae is the job of the intervertebral discs.

q: The knee is described as a modified hinge. What makes it modified?
o: It also rotates when it is bent
It glides side to side when it is straight
It moves freely in all three planes
It abducts when fully extended
e: Unlike a simple hinge, the knee rotates when bent, which is why the hamstrings and sartorius can rotate the tibia. Movement in all three planes belongs to ball-and-socket joints.

q: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is which type of synovial joint?
o: Pivot
Hinge
Ball-and-socket
Saddle
e: It is a saddle joint: one bone sits on the other like a rider on a saddle, allowing back and forth, side to side and a little rotation. Pivot examples are the atlantoaxial and proximal radioulnar joints.

q: The ACL is mostly collagen with very little elastin. What does that suit it to?
o: Stretching and recoiling during deep knee bends
Absorbing shock between the femur and tibia
Healing quickly after it is sprained
Resisting strong forces to stabilise the knee
e: Collagen gives tensile strength and elastin gives elastic recoil, so a collagen-rich ACL resists strong forces well. Ligaments have poor vascularity and heal poorly, so quick healing is wrong.

q: A client asks why their sprained ankle ligament is so slow to heal. What is the accurate answer?
o: Ligaments contain very little collagen
Ligaments have a limited blood supply
Ligaments have no nerve supply at all
Ligaments are cartilage, not fibrous tissue
e: Ligaments have poor vascularity, so they heal and adapt slowly. They are fibrous, mainly collagen, and send sensory input that aids proprioception, so the other options are wrong.

q: What is the difference between osteokinematics and arthrokinematics?
o: Osteokinematics is bone movement; arthrokinematics is joint-surface movement
Osteokinematics is inside the joint; arthrokinematics is the visible bone movement
They are two names for the same joint movement
Osteokinematics is synovial joints only; arthrokinematics is all joints
e: Osteokinematics is the vocabulary of flexion, extension and so on. Arthrokinematics is roll, slide and spin between the joint surfaces while that happens, and it cannot be seen.

q: Why do roll and glide usually happen together at a joint such as the knee?
o: A roll alone would soon take the bone out of its socket
The glide produces the range and the roll keeps it centred
Roll happens only in open chain movement, glide in closed
The glide is needed to produce synovial fluid
e: A roll cannot go far on its own without the bone leaving its socket. The glide keeps the surfaces centred while the roll produces the range; the second option swaps the two jobs.

q: A client feels a pinch at the front of the ankle when stretching the calf into dorsiflexion. What should you do?
o: Push through it, since a tight calf is the usual cause
Stop, and mobilise the ankle's glide first
Hold the stretch longer until the pinch eases off
Keep stretching but add foam rolling to the calf
e: Never work through a pinch. The problem is often the talus not gliding, so mobilise the glide first, after which the calf stretch can be done without it. Tension at end of range responds to patience; a pinch is two structures meeting and responds by getting injured.

q: A client with shoulder pain has been told their tendon is being pinched under the bone. What is the accurate reply?
o: Surgery to remove the bone is the most reliable fix
Rest until the pinching stops is the safest option
Most such pain responds to progressive loading
Scapular exercises are needed to prevent the pinching
e: There is little evidence that impingement is the main cause of shoulder pain: removing bone surgically does no better than a placebo operation, and most such pain responds to progressive loading. Train scapular control for overhead strength, not to prevent impingement.

q: Why is a press-up a closed chain exercise?
o: It works several muscle groups and joints at the same time
It uses body weight rather than an external load
The hands stay fixed while the elbows and shoulders move
The body is held in a straight line throughout
e: Closed chain means the distal segments are fixed against an immovable surface. Several muscle groups are often involved, but that is a feature, not the definition.

q: A client squats well, but one quadriceps is clearly weaker and stronger muscles compensate for it. What is the right call?
o: Add more squat volume until the weak side catches up
Replace all closed chain work with machine exercises
Keep to closed chain work, since it is always better
Add open chain work loading the weak muscle directly
e: Open chain work loads one muscle directly, which is what you want when the closed chain pattern lets stronger muscles compensate. Neither kind is better; train the pattern, then address the weak link.

q: A client worries their back will be damaged if it ever rounds while lifting a bag of shopping. What is the accurate reply?
o: Little evidence links a rounded back when lifting to pain
Any rounding under load damages the discs
Rounding is safe only below a set weight
Rounding causes back pain unless the core is braced hard
e: Neutral spine is a sensible default for heavy lifts, not proof that bending is dangerous. Beliefs that the back is fragile predict slower recovery. Osteoporosis is the exception, where high degrees of loaded flexion should be avoided.

q: A pain-free client is alarmed that a scan showed a disc bulge. What is the accurate reply?
o: A bulge means they should stop lifting until it heals
A bulge explains any back pain they get in future
Disc bulges are common in people with no pain
A bulge shows their discs have stopped adapting
e: Disc bulges show up in about 30% of pain-free 20-year-olds and over 80% of pain-free 80-year-olds. Discs adapt to load like other tissues.

q: Which of these is one of NASM's five body regions for observation?
o: The elbow and wrist
The thoracic spine and ribs
The hip and knee together
The lumbo-pelvic-hip complex
e: The five are head and cervical spine, shoulders and thoracic spine, the lumbo-pelvic-hip complex, the knee, and the foot and ankle. The thoracic spine is grouped with the shoulders, not the ribs.

q: What else are the five body regions used for, beyond observation?
o: As the five spinal regions, from the cervical to the coccyx
As the list of joints that are synovial
As the order in which to warm up the body
As checkpoints for posture and movement analysis
e: The same five kinetic chain checkpoints are used in the postural assessments, and the lunge is analysed segment by segment through them, so one framework covers both.

q: Which term means positioned on the opposite side of the body?
o: Ipsilateral
Contralateral
Distal
Lateral
e: Contralateral is the opposite side and ipsilateral the same side. Lateral means towards the outside, and distal means farthest from the centre or point of reference.

q: A client lies face up for a bench press. What is that position called?
o: Prone
Supine
Lateral
Posterior
e: Supine is face up, as in a crunch or bench press. Prone is face down, as in a superman or a plank.

q: How does a movement relate to its axis?
o: It slides along an axis that lies inside its plane
It turns around an axis parallel to its plane
It turns around an axis at right angles to its plane
It has an axis only when the joint is under load
e: Each movement happens in a plane and turns around an axis at right angles to it, as a car wheel turns around its axle.

q: A lateral raise is called a frontal plane movement. On what basis are movements named this way?
o: The axis they turn around
The muscle that drives them
The joint where they occur
The plane they happen in
e: Movements are named after the plane they happen in. The axis runs at right angles to that plane, so naming by axis would be the tempting mix-up.

q: Hip flexion can happen two ways. Which one is the hip hinge?
o: Pelvis on femur: the femur stays still, the pelvis moves
Femur on pelvis: the pelvis stays still and the femur moves
Both at once, which is why it is called a hinge
Neither, since the hip hinge is really a form of hip extension
e: The hip hinge is pelvis on femur. Both ways count as hip flexion because both decrease the angle between the femur and the pelvis.

q: During the lowering phase of a squat, what is happening at the hip?
o: Hip flexion
Hip extension
Hip abduction
Hip internal rotation
e: Lowering decreases the angle between the femur and the pelvis, so it is hip flexion. Hip extension is the lifting phase.

q: What is eversion of the foot?
o: Turning the sole inwards, weight to the outer edge
Pointing the foot, as at the top of a calf raise
Bringing the top of the foot towards the shin
Turning the sole outwards, weight to the inner edge
e: Eversion turns the sole outwards, shifting weight to the inner edge while the outer edge lifts. Inversion is the reverse; the last two are plantar flexion and dorsiflexion, in the sagittal plane.

q: Which group of movements happens in the frontal plane?
o: Flexion, extension, dorsiflexion and plantar flexion
Rotation plus horizontal abduction and adduction
Abduction, adduction, lateral flexion and inversion
Forearm pronation and supination, spinal rotation
e: Frontal plane movements go side to side: abduction, adduction, lateral flexion, eversion and inversion. Flexion and extension are sagittal; rotation, horizontal movements and forearm pronation and supination are transverse.

q: With the feet planted, a client turns the hips to the right. What happens at each hip?
o: Right hip rotates externally, left hip internally
Both hips rotate internally together
Both hips rotate externally
Left hip rotates externally, right hip internally
e: Turning the hips to the right over fixed femurs produces external rotation of the left hip and internal rotation of the right. Turning left reverses it.

q: A client presses dumbbells with the elbows tucked close to the torso rather than out wide. What movement is that at the shoulder?
o: Horizontal adduction of the shoulder, in the transverse plane
Shoulder abduction, in the frontal plane
Shoulder flexion and extension, in the sagittal plane
Shoulder internal rotation, in the transverse plane
e: With the elbows out wide, a press or fly is horizontal adduction in the transverse plane. With the elbows close to the torso it becomes shoulder flexion and extension in the sagittal plane.

q: Which of these is given as a movement in all three planes at once?
o: Picking up a child and turning to set them down
Walking in a straight line, facing forwards
A lateral raise with dumbbells
A biceps curl with the elbows fixed at the sides
e: Walking while looking around, dancing, ball sports and picking up a child and turning are the multiplanar examples. Plain walking happens mainly in the sagittal plane.

q: Why train in all three planes?
o: Single-plane training is what causes muscle imbalances
Life and sport load all three, and tissue adapts
Multiplanar work burns more energy in each session
The sagittal plane is the least safe plane to load
e: Train in all three planes because life and sport load all three, and tissues adapt to what they are exposed to.

q: The muscular system links which two systems?
o: The cardiovascular and respiratory systems
The endocrine and nervous systems
The nervous and skeletal systems
The skeletal and respiratory systems
e: The muscular system links the nervous and skeletal systems: nerves move muscles, and muscles move bones.

q: Besides producing movement and supporting the skeleton, what does skeletal muscle do?
o: Produces heat, helping maintain homeostasis
Produces red blood cells in its fibres
Stores the body's reserves of minerals
Secretes the fluid that lubricates the joints
e: Skeletal muscle contracts to move, supports the skeleton and produces heat. Blood cells and mineral storage belong to the skeleton, and lubrication to synovial fluid.

q: What does the sarcoplasmic reticulum release to trigger contraction?
o: Potassium
ATP
Acetylcholine
Calcium
e: The impulse makes the sarcoplasmic reticulum release calcium, which lets the myosin heads bind to actin. Acetylcholine is released earlier, into the neuromuscular junction.

q: What role does ATP play in a muscle contraction?
o: It carries the impulse across the neuromuscular junction
It powers the power stroke and lets the myosin heads detach
It is released by the sarcoplasmic reticulum to start binding
It carries the action potential down the motor neuron
e: ATP powers the power stroke and is also needed for the myosin heads to detach and reset. Acetylcholine crosses the junction, calcium is released by the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and sodium and potassium carry the action potential.

q: What is the primary purpose of small motor units?
o: Stabilising the body, as in upright posture
Moving the body, as in running or jumping
Producing large forces quickly
Recruiting Type II fibres for speed and power
e: Small motor units supply small Type I fibres, are fatigue resistant and produce small forces slowly, so their job is stabilising. Large units, with Type II fibres, move the body.

q: Soleus is rich in Type I fibres. What determines a muscle's fibre-type mix?
o: Its size
How far it sits from the heart
How long it is
Its function and genetics
e: Fibre type follows function and genetics, not muscle size. Postural muscles such as soleus are rich in Type I fibres.

q: What does the all-or-nothing principle state?
o: A muscle either contracts fully or tears under load
An action potential activates every fibre in that motor unit
Every motor unit in the whole muscle fires at the same moment
Contraction strength depends only on muscle size
e: If the impulse is strong enough to trigger an action potential, all fibres supplied by that nerve contract fully; if not, none do. It applies to the motor unit, not the whole muscle.

q: If each fibre contracts fully or not at all, how does a whole muscle vary its force?
o: By each fibre contracting partly when less force is needed
By changing the length of the tendon
By switching fibres between Type I and Type II
Through which motor units fire, how many, and how fast
e: Whole-muscle force depends on which motor units are recruited, how many are active and how fast they fire, called rate coding. Rate of force development depends heavily on firing rates.

q: What does Henneman's size principle state?
o: Units are recruited smallest to largest as force demand rises
Large motor units are recruited first whenever the load is heavy
Only large motor units work above moderate loads
Motor units are recruited at random to share fatigue
e: Recruitment follows size order. The small, slow units are recruited first every rep, without exception, even when the large units are called in on rep one of a heavy set.

q: A deconditioned client cannot yet load a barbell. How can you still recruit their large motor units?
o: You cannot until they can handle a heavy load
Slow, light sets stopped well short of fatigue
Body-weight work done fast or close to fatigue
Low-effort machine work to isolate each muscle
e: Speed raises the force requirement and fatigue brings in large units as small ones tire, and both are available with body weight. A deconditioned client does not need a heavy bar.

q: For muscle growth, how close to failure should most sets finish?
o: Always to failure, since growth depends on reaching it
About halfway, well short of fatigue
A rep or two short, failure as a deliberate choice
To failure on the first set, then stop
e: Growth increases as sets finish closer to failure, but going all the way adds little over stopping a rep or two short. Novices should stop further from failure, because technique breaks down near it.

q: Why are Type I fibres called red fibres?
o: They hold more haemoglobin than Type II fibres
They are rich in myoglobin, which binds oxygen
They store more glycogen than Type II fibres
They contain more actin than myosin
e: Myoglobin is similar to haemoglobin, the red oxygen-carrying pigment in red blood cells, which is why Type I fibres are red. Haemoglobin sits in red blood cells, not in the fibre.

q: How does training of almost any kind change fibre types?
o: IIx fibres shift towards IIa, fast and oxidative
Most Type II fibres convert into slow Type I fibres
Type I fibres shift towards IIx
IIa fibres shift towards IIx
e: Training converts IIx towards IIa, which is fast and oxidative and sits between the other two types. Conversion between Type II and Type I in humans is small and disputed, so proportions are largely inherited.

q: After age 50, muscle mass is lost at an average rate of about:
o: 0.1 to 0.2 per cent a year
1 to 2 per cent a year
5 per cent a year
10 per cent a year
e: After 50, muscle mass falls by an average of 1 to 2 per cent a year. Changes are small from 30 to 50, and resistance training is highly beneficial against the loss.

q: Plotting strength against age gives parallel lines for trained, active and sedentary people. What does that show?
o: Training raises the level you decline from
Training slows the rate of decline
Training stops decline until about 70
Training helps only people who start while young
e: The lines are parallel, so training does not slow the rate of decline; it raises the level you decline from. People in their nineties still gain muscle and strength.

q: Which pair of muscles both have pennate fibres?
o: Biceps and sartorius
Deltoid and rectus femoris
Deltoid and biceps
Sartorius and rectus femoris
e: The deltoid and rectus femoris have pennate fibres, angled onto a central tendon like the barbs of a feather. The biceps and sartorius are the parallel examples.

q: What does a parallel fibre arrangement, as in the biceps or sartorius, favour?
o: Force, by packing more fibres into the space
Range of motion and speed of shortening
Fatigue resistance, through more capillaries
Joint stability at the expense of range
e: Fibres parallel to the line of pull favour range and speed of shortening. Pennate fibres pack more in and favour force over range.

q: Why does an eccentric action followed straight away by a concentric one produce more force?
o: Extra motor units recruited through fatigue
Lactate building up in the working muscle
Stored elastic energy and the stretch reflex
A longer amortisation phase at the turnaround
e: Elastic energy stored in tendon and connective tissue, and the stretch reflex firing on rapid lengthening, both add force. If the amortisation phase drags, the energy is lost as heat and the reflex contribution goes.

q: A client's squat has gone up a lot, but their tennis serve has not improved at all. What does that suggest the limit is?
o: Their maximal strength, which needs more load
Their absolute strength, which is fixed
Their muscle size, which lags behind
How much force they can use in the movement
e: If getting stronger changes nothing, the limit is optimal usable strength, the force they can apply given their coordination and control. More maximal strength will not help; the work is coordination and control.

q: Most sporting skills finish in under 0.18 seconds. Why does that matter for training?
o: Only Type I fibres can fire within that time
Maximal force is reached well within that time
Movements that fast rely on stored elastic energy alone
Peak force takes 0.3 to 0.4 s, so its rate of rise matters
e: Producing maximal force takes 0.3 to 0.4 seconds, so a sporting movement never reaches its maximum. How quickly force rises, the rate of force development, is what counts.

q: A weak, untrained client wants to become more explosive. What is the quickest route?
o: Plyometrics only, since strength will not transfer
Maximal reactive jump testing in the first session
Light, slow work until usable strength catches up
Get stronger, lifting with intent to move fast
e: In weaker or untrained people, getting stronger is the quickest way to become more explosive. Once someone is strong, extra maximal strength transfers less. Maximal reactive work should not be tested on day one.

q: An athlete delivers well under half their maximum force in the time the movement allows. What should they train?
o: Maximal strength
Rate of force development
Muscle size
Absolute strength
e: A large explosive strength deficit means the limit is access, not force, so train rate of force development; more maximal strength will not help. A small deficit, where the maximum is simply low, calls for maximal strength.

q: What distinguishes sarcoplasmic hypertrophy from myofibrillar hypertrophy?
o: It adds non-contractile content, with less strength per size
It adds contractile machinery, so strength rises in proportion
It occurs only in Type I fibres, never in Type II
It happens only when sets are taken to failure
e: Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy expands the non-contractile content of the cell; myofibrillar hypertrophy adds contractile machinery, so strength rises in proportion to size. The research on the split is divided.

q: A client asks whether sets of fifteen build 'sarcoplasmic' size and sets of five 'functional' size. What is the accurate answer?
o: Yes, choosing the rep range reliably selects the type
No, sarcoplasmic hypertrophy does not exist
Rep range may bias it, as a tendency, not a dial
Only low-rep sets produce any real growth
e: Both kinds have some support, but there is little evidence you can reliably select one by rep range. Heavier work may bias myofibrillar and high volume sarcoplasmic, as a tendency only.

q: Why does the nervous system organise muscles into synergies?
o: It lets each muscle be trained in isolation
It spreads fatigue across the fibre types
It simplifies movement into functional units
It stops antagonists working during a lift
e: Muscles rarely work alone. Working in groups under nervous system control simplifies movement and lets muscles and joints operate as a functional unit.

q: What makes muscle synergies more fluent and automatic?
o: Stretching each muscle in the group
Training each muscle separately to failure
Practising good movement patterns
Adding load every session
e: Practising good movement patterns makes synergies more fluent and automatic. Training muscles one at a time does not build the group coordination.

q: In the lunge, what do the hamstrings do at the knee?
o: Stabilise it as the quadriceps extend it
Extend it on the way up
Rotate it inwards to keep it tracking over the toes
Flex it to lower the body
e: At the knee the quadriceps extend on the way up and the hamstrings stabilise, with the knee tracking the toes.

q: A calf raise uses the ball of the foot as the fulcrum. Which class of lever is it?
o: First, with the fulcrum in the middle
Third, with the effort in the middle
Second, with the resistance in the middle
Third, with the fulcrum at the ankle joint
e: The ball of the foot is the fulcrum, body weight the resistance and the calf the effort, with the resistance in the middle: a second-class lever, like a wheelbarrow.

q: Most human limbs are third-class levers. What does that arrangement trade?
o: Speed, in exchange for extra force
Force, in exchange for speed and range
Range, in exchange for joint stability
Nothing; it multiplies force like a wheelbarrow
e: In a third-class lever the effort sits closest to the fulcrum, so the muscle must produce more force than the load and gets speed and range in exchange. The wheelbarrow is second class, which multiplies force.

q: A client walks from pavement onto sand and changes their walking pattern. In what order do the nervous system's three functions occur?
o: Sensory, then integrative, then motor
Motor, then sensory, then integrative
Integrative, then sensory, then motor
Sensory, then motor, with no integrative step
e: The change underfoot is sensed, then analysed and interpreted, and the motor response is the changed walking pattern.

q: What is the nervous system's integrative function?
o: Sensing changes inside and outside the body
Making the muscle contract in response
Carrying signals out to the muscles
Interpreting sensory information to make decisions
e: Integrative is the analysis and interpretation that allows proper decision-making. Sensing changes is the sensory function and the contraction is the motor response.

q: What does the peripheral nervous system include?
o: 12 cranial nerves, 31 spinal nerve pairs and the receptors
31 cranial nerves, 12 spinal nerve pairs and the brain stem
The brain, the brain stem and the spinal cord
The interneurons within the spinal cord and brain
e: The peripheral system is 12 cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves and the sensory receptors. The brain and spinal cord are the central system, where interneurons also sit.

q: What two jobs do peripheral nerves do?
o: Interpret sensory input and decide on a response
Carry commands out and bring sensory information back
Store motor patterns and control reflexes centrally
Produce electrolytes and conduct the impulse
e: Peripheral nerves carry commands out (motor function) and bring information back through sensory receptors (sensory function). Interpreting input and deciding is the central nervous system's job.

q: Which part of a neuron carries impulses to other neurons or to muscles and organs?
o: The dendrites
The axon
The cell body
The nucleus
e: The axon carries impulses out to other neurons, muscles and organs. Dendrites gather information into the neuron, and the cell body holds the nucleus and controls the cell.

q: Which of these are all electrolytes needed for nerve and muscle function?
o: Sodium, potassium, magnesium and water
Sodium, calcium, iron and zinc
Sodium, potassium, chloride and magnesium
Potassium, calcium, chloride and blood glucose
e: The main electrolytes are sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium and magnesium. Water is the solvent they dissolve in, not an electrolyte.

q: Afferent pathways carry information in which direction?
o: Out from the central nervous system to the muscles
Between neurons, only inside the brain and spinal cord
From one muscle to another, bypassing the spinal cord
To the central nervous system; they are sensory
e: Afferent pathways are sensory, carrying information to the central nervous system. Efferent pathways are motor, and interneurons pass impulses between the two inside the brain and spinal cord.

q: Proprioception travels which route, and what does training it improve?
o: Afferent; balance, coordination and posture
Efferent; balance, coordination and upright posture
Afferent; pain tolerance and flexibility
Efferent; maximal strength and power
e: Proprioception, the sense of where the body's parts are, travels the afferent route. Training it improves balance, coordination and posture and lets the body adapt without conscious thought.

q: A client says the more their knee hurts, the more damage there must be. What is the accurate reply?
o: Pain closely tracks the amount of tissue damage
Pain means the knee must be rested until it stops
Pain is protective, not a measure of damage
Pain comes straight from the nociceptors, unfiltered
e: Whether nociceptor signals become pain is decided by the brain, which weighs context, mood and past experience. Describe what you see as a capacity to build, never as damage.

q: A client with back pain mentions new numbness around the groin and trouble passing urine. What do you do?
o: Refer them to their GP within the week
Carry on with gentle mobility work
Stop the session and review it next time
Stop and send them to A&E the same day
e: Back pain with numbness around the groin or back passage or new trouble passing urine is an emergency. Red flags prompt referral; they do not diagnose.

q: Which statement about the sympathetic and parasympathetic branches is accurate?
o: Only one branch is active at any moment
Both are always active; the balance shifts
The sympathetic branch switches off during rest
The parasympathetic branch works only during sleep
e: Both branches are active all the time; exercise, stress and rest shift the balance. Sympathetic is fight or flight, parasympathetic rest and digest.

q: Which part of polyvagal theory is the most contested?
o: That the two autonomic branches exist
Its evolutionary history
That slow breathing raises vagal HRV
That stress withdraws parasympathetic activity
e: The evolutionary story, that a myelinated ventral vagal complex is uniquely mammalian, is the weakest part. The two branches, parasympathetic withdrawal under stress and slow breathing raising vagal HRV all survive without the theory.

q: A client's RSA rises after five minutes of slow breathing. What can you conclude about their autonomic state?
o: They have moved into the ventral vagal state
Their sympathetic branch has switched off
Little, since breathing alone changes RSA
Any overtraining they had has now cleared
e: RSA varies with the rate and depth of breathing, so it is not a clean index of vagal tone. Do not treat a breathing-driven change in RSA as proof of a state change.

q: During a breathing drill, a client starts to panic and discloses past trauma. What do you do?
o: Stop, help them settle, signpost to a professional
Carry on, as the drill is regulating their nervous system
Talk them through the memory so they can release it
Switch to a harder drill to take their mind off it
e: If a client dissociates, panics or discloses trauma, stop, help them settle and signpost to a mental health professional. Do not frame sessions as treating their nervous system.

q: A client is just learning a skill and their performance is inconsistent. Which stage is this, and what should you do?
o: Associative; refine through practice and feedback
Autonomous; teach new versions of the skill
Cognitive; add load to stabilise the pattern
Cognitive; simple instructions and smaller steps
e: Inconsistent performance marks the cognitive stage, where the response is simple instructions and breaking the skill into smaller steps. Refining with feedback is the associative stage.

q: A beginner improved quickly at a new skill for a few weeks and has now stalled. What is the most useful explanation?
o: The programme has stopped working and needs changing
They have reached their natural ceiling for the skill
Their early neural gains have now worn off
Coordination comes fast; control is the slow half
e: Coordination, the correct relative pattern, is learned fast; control, the timing and force of each segment, slowly. Telling a client that is more useful than changing their programme.

q: A beginner golfer locks their wrists and elbows and swings their arms like a pendulum. What should you do?
o: Cue them to relax every joint straight away
Correct it at once, since the rigidity is an error
Demonstrate one expert swing until they copy it
Unfreeze one joint at a time, as the skill needs
e: Freezing joints is a coping strategy, not an error. Cueing them to relax a frozen joint removes the strategy before they have the control to replace it.

q: A client already has a rough idea of what a movement looks like. How should you teach it?
o: Try words first, then show several versions
Demonstrate one ideal version over and over again
Avoid demonstrating, since it harms learning
Show only your own way of doing the movement
e: Demonstrations help most when the learner has no idea of the movement. With a rough idea, try verbal instruction and, if they struggle, show several versions. Harm from too much demonstration is one expert's view, not established.

q: A client who trained well for years is coming back after a long layoff. What should you tell them before the first session?
o: They will move well but tire quickly, as skill outlasts conditioning
Every quality will have faded equally, so start again from zero
They will probably have lost their technique but kept most of their endurance
Their strength will be gone but their aerobic fitness will be intact
e: Neuromuscular adaptation, especially coordination, survives for years, while endurance fades within two to four weeks. Tell them before the first session, because it is the opposite of what they expect.

q: Two clients follow the same programme for twelve weeks and one improves far more than the other. Which principle explains this?
o: Homeostasis: the client who improved less holds conditions steadier
Individuality: responses vary in size between people, largely through genetics
Reversibility: the client who improved less must have missed sessions
Specificity: the client who improved less must have trained a different quality
e: Individuality says the direction of the response is predictable but its size varies between people, and identical twins respond more alike than unrelated people. Tell clients this in advance.

q: A client has one leg immobilised in a brace after surgery and asks whether training the other leg is worth it. What do you tell them?
o: No: training one limb weakens the immobilised limb further
No: specificity means the untrained limb gains nothing at all
Yes: the untrained limb gains roughly 8 to 12% in strength
Yes: the untrained limb gains roughly as much as the trained one
e: This is cross-education, one of the limits of specificity. It is useful exactly when one limb is immobilised.

q: A client is taking three weeks off with no training and worries their strength will be gone when they return. What do the detraining data say?
o: It holds for about two to three weeks, then declines slowly
It is largely lost within the first four or five days
It holds for years, like coordination and other skill
It halves in three weeks and returns only at the rate it was built
e: Strength holds for about two to three weeks, then declines slowly, and comes back faster than it was first built. Endurance fades sooner, within two to four weeks.

q: Motor units are always recruited smallest to largest. What are the three ways to reach the largest units?
o: Use isolation exercises, long pauses, or very slow lowering
Lift heavy, lift slowly, or lift on an unstable surface
Lift only near maximum, since nothing else reaches them
Lift heavy, lift fast, or lift until tired
e: You cannot skip motor units, so the largest are reached only by heavy load, high speed or fatigue. Each route gives a different result.

q: A client used to high-intensity classes says a slow, exact groundwork session was not a real workout. Which principle answers them?
o: Renting is not owning, so the session was only a warm-up
You cannot skip motor units, so only heavy work counts
Precision is the workload: being exact is the stimulus
Programme patterns, not muscles, so intensity matters less
e: The effort of being exact is the stimulus, not a preliminary to it. Tell clients this before the session, or they will not put the effort in.

q: Your plan says a client moves to the next level in week six. In week six they still cannot do the current level well. What do you do?
o: Move them on but halve the volume for the first week
Stay at the current level until they can do it well
Move them on anyway, since the plan was written around their goal
Restart the whole plan from week one
e: The client earns the next level, and the test for moving on is something they can do, not a date in the calendar.

q: Which of these progression rules lets the client earn the next level?
o: Progress every second Monday, as set out in the written plan
Progress after two complete weeks in a row at the current level
Progress after four weeks, whatever the attendance has been
Progress whenever the client says the sessions feel boring
e: The test for moving on is something the client does, not a date in the calendar. Progressing on a condition such as two complete weeks in a row lets consistency earn the increase, and a hard fortnight delays it.

q: Which progression unit belongs to cardiorespiratory training rather than resistance training?
o: Set
Phase
Stage
Repetition
e: Cardio progresses through stages, resistance through phases. They are two separate systems with two separate sets of words.

q: How is resistance training intensity described, as opposed to cardio intensity?
o: By the talk test, as with cardio
By acute variables: sets, reps, load, tempo, rest
By training zone, calculated from a percentage of heart rate reserve
By ventilatory threshold, VT1 and VT2
e: Zones, defined by ventilatory thresholds, apply to cardio only. A set of squats does not have a zone.

q: A deconditioned client has been doing steady walks below VT1 for six weeks. What tells you they are ready to start Stage 2 intervals?
o: They reach 75% of their predicted maximum heart rate while walking
Six weeks have passed, which is the standard length of Stage 1
They can hold zone 1 for 30 minutes, three times a week
They have completed a submaximal VO2max test
e: The gate to Stage 2 is holding zone 1 for 30 minutes three times a week. A deconditioned client may need two to three months to get there.

q: A client new to intervals has started Stage 2 with one minute of zone 2 work against three minutes of zone 1 recovery. How do you progress them before adding total volume?
o: Lengthen each work interval to five minutes at the same ratio
Add a fourth interval session to the week
Move some of the work intervals up into zone 3
Tighten the work-to-rest ratio from 1:3 to 1:2 to 1:1
e: Progress by tightening the ratio before adding total volume, and raise the workload through speed or incline. Zone 3 belongs to Stage 3, which needs VT1 and VT2 recorded.

q: What is the status of NASM's cap of 10% added cardio volume a week?
o: A reasonable default, not a proven injury shield
Too cautious: the evidence supports about 25% a week
Superseded by a rule of doubling volume every four weeks
A proven way to prevent running injuries in novices
e: The 10% rule is a sensible default, but one large trial in novice runners found it made no difference to injuries.

q: A client without a heart rate monitor is working at a pace where they can manage only short phrases. Which zone are they in?
o: Zone 4, above VT2
Zone 1, below VT1
Zone 3, between the midpoint and VT2
Zone 2, between VT1 and the midpoint
e: Short phrases only marks zone 3, at RPE 7 to 8. In zone 2 continuous talking is becoming hard; in zone 4 speech is impossible or single words.

q: What is the status of the order in NASM's corrective exercise continuum (inhibit, lengthen, activate, integrate)?
o: Supported by trials for clients with muscle imbalances only
An organising order, with nothing to show the order is necessary
Proven for beginners only, and optional for experienced lifters
A proven sequence: skipping a step stops the later steps from working
e: The continuum gives a session a clear order, but nothing shows the order is necessary or that a corrective phase beats starting sensible strength training.

q: How does static stretching improve range of motion?
o: By switching the muscle off through autogenic and reciprocal inhibition
By measurably lengthening the muscle fibres over weeks
Mostly lower stiffness at first, then more stretch tolerance
By releasing adhesions and scar tissue in the fascia
e: Short-term gains are mostly lower stiffness, though reviews differ on how much comes from tolerating more stretch; over weeks, tolerance adds to it. Stretching does not measurably lengthen the fibres.

q: A new client has poor balance and a rounded posture. NASM would rule out dynamic stretching for them. What do you do in the warm-up?
o: Leave out the warm-up and start with light working sets
Use a dynamic warm-up, scaled in range and speed
Leave out dynamic work until a corrective phase is complete
Use only static stretching until the posture has improved
e: The gate behind corrective work is NASM's own. A dynamic warm-up suits almost everyone when range and speed are scaled.

q: A client wants to get stronger. Which prescription matches the evidence?
o: Loads of 50 to 70% 1RM, 1 to 3 sets, a single session each week
Loads of about 80% 1RM or more, 2 to 3 sets, twice or more a week
Any load, as long as every set is taken all the way to true failure
Loads of 30 to 45% 1RM lifted fast, 3 to 6 sets, twice a week
e: The ACSM 2026 position stand gives about 80% 1RM or more, 2 to 3 sets, on two or more sessions a week for strength. True failure is not needed.

q: A client training for muscle growth rests five minutes between sets of 10 and keeps running out of session time. What do you tell them?
o: Keep five minutes, since longer rest keeps building more muscle
At least 60 to 90 seconds is enough for growth; longer adds little
Rest 3 to 5 minutes, as the evidence gives for all resistance work
Cut rest to 20 seconds, since the fatigue is what drives growth
e: Rest has two cases. For muscle growth at least 60 to 90 seconds is enough and longer adds little; 3 to 5 minutes is for heavy strength work near maximum, so the next set can be just as heavy.

q: A client has a powerlifting competition in two weeks. How do you taper?
o: Stop training entirely for the two weeks before the competition
Keep the volume the same and cut the intensity by about half
Train once a week only, and raise the volume of that one session
Cut volume by 40 to 60% for one to two weeks, keeping intensity
e: The evidence gives a clearer rule than either taper model: cut volume by about 40 to 60% for one to two weeks and keep intensity and frequency.

q: What is the status of Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome as a model of training?
o: The evidence is against it as a model of training
It is well supported for beginners and less so for advanced lifters
It is untested but explains tapering and deloads well
It is the best-supported model of how training adaptation works
e: GAS is graded poor as a training model, and it explains none of tapering, deloads or feeling better after doing less. The principles often derived from it stand on their own evidence.

q: A client feels worse in week three of a hard block and better in week four after you cut the volume. Which model explains this?
o: Reversibility: the block's gains were lost and then rebuilt
General Adaptation Syndrome: week three was the exhaustion stage
Fitness-fatigue: fatigue fades faster than fitness
The SAID principle: the body adapted to the lighter demand
e: Each session gives a lasting fitness gain and a short-lived fatigue cost, and performance is the sum. GAS alone explains none of this.

q: A client can reach a deep split squat but the position wobbles and changes every rep. They want to add load. What do you do?
o: Add reps before load, since reps condition it safely
Correct the position before loading it
Add speed, since faster reps hide the wobble
Add load now, since load will stabilise the position
e: A movement the client can produce but not hold, repeat or vary is rented. Correction is for rented movement; conditioning is for owned movement.

q: A client's half kneeling position keeps failing. Where do you look first?
o: One level down, at tall kneeling
One level up, at standing, to see whether it disappears
Nowhere: drop the position and use a machine instead
At the feet and ankles, which usually cause half kneeling faults
e: When something fails at a higher level, drop to the level below and find what is missing there. A failing half kneeling is often a tall kneeling problem, and a failing tall kneeling often a hip extension problem.

q: A lean, well-trained athlete starts shaking in a groundwork position and wants to back off. What do you tell them?
o: Shaking means their strength is poor, so switch to heavier work
Shaking shows the position is too advanced, so regress straight away
Shaking is the nervous system learning to stabilise, not failure
Shaking is a sign of low fuel, so they should eat before continuing
e: Say so, or clients read the shaking as weakness and back off just when the learning is happening. Strong athletes fail in these positions because the demand is not the one they are conditioned for.

t: Programming for a client with a larger body
q: You want to include self-myofascial work for a client with a larger body. How do you set it up?
o: Do the same work seated or standing, avoiding the floor
Do it on the floor, helping the client down and up
Replace it with a machine circuit
Leave it out, since it can only be done lying on a roller
e: Getting to and from the floor is mechanically hard at higher body mass and a dignity issue. Everything SMR does can be done seated or standing, so designing around it costs nothing.

t: Programming for a client with a larger body
q: Early in a session, a client with a larger body becomes flushed and distressed. How do you treat it?
o: As a sign to lower the intensity and carry on
As a soft signal to push through, since it usually passes
As a reason to move the rest of the session onto the floor
As a reason to stop the session
e: More mass makes more heat and has less surface area for its size to lose it. Use cooler rooms, more frequent drinks breaks and shorter starting sessions, and treat early flushing or distress as a reason to stop.

q: A client does 150 minutes of resistance training a week and no aerobic work. Do they meet the activity guidelines?
o: Yes, provided at least two of the sessions are vigorous
No: resistance training does not count towards any part of them
No: resistance training does not replace the aerobic minutes
Yes: the 150 minutes can come from either kind of training
e: The aerobic minutes (150 to 300 moderate or 75 to 150 vigorous) and strength on two or more days are two separate requirements, not one total.

q: A client says their five-minute walks between meetings do not count because they are shorter than ten minutes. What do you tell them?
o: They count: the 10-minute minimum bout was removed in 2018
They count only if the walks reach vigorous intensity
They are right: only bouts of ten minutes or more count towards it
They count only once the day's total reaches 10,000 steps
e: The 10-minute minimum no longer exists: all movement counts, however short. For most clients five minutes is the unit they actually have.

q: In a weight-loss programme, what is the real argument for resistance training over aerobic work?
o: It burns far more calories per session
It produces more scale weight loss
It keeps or increases lean mass
It produces more fat loss than aerobic work
e: Aerobic work gives more scale weight and fat loss, but no lean mass improvement. Load is the signal that keeps muscle in a deficit.

q: A client wants to do hard running intervals and heavy leg work on the same day. How do you arrange it?
o: Run first, then go straight into the heavy lifts
Put them back to back, since the two do not interfere at all
Separate them by a few hours where possible
Never train both kinds in the same week
e: Cardio and lifting interfere little for most clients, but power suffers most when both are in one session, so separate hard running and heavy leg work by a few hours where possible.

q: A well-trained client and a less-trained client both do aerobic threshold work. How long does each need before repeating it?
o: About 24 hours for the well trained, about 48 for the less trained
About 12 hours for the well trained, about 24 for the less trained
7 to 14 days for both
36 to 96 hours for both
e: Aerobic threshold work needs 12 to 24 hours. Strength needs 36 to 96 hours, and 7 to 14 days applies to a first, unfamiliar eccentric bout.

q: A client's waking heart rate has sat about 5 beats above their usual for three days. What is the right response?
o: Refer to a GP for suspected overtraining syndrome
Ask about it and check their RPE
Ignore it, since several beats is normal day-to-day spread
Stop all training for a month to be safe
e: Normal day-to-day spread is several beats, but a rise of about 5 or more lasting two or three days is worth asking about. No single marker diagnoses overtraining.

q: A client's orthostatic test shows the gap between lying and standing heart rate widening, with a steep rise in the standing value. What does it mean?
o: The test was done wrongly and should be repeated lying only
Nothing, since standing is always higher than lying
The body is struggling, so reduce the load now
The systems are working well, so progress the load
e: A narrow or closing gap is a good response to training. A widening gap with a steep standing rise means reduce the load now.

q: A client's wearable shows their heart rate variability dropped sharply this morning. How do you use it?
o: Cancel today's session, since one low reading shows overtraining
Double the session's intensity to restore the variability
Ignore HRV entirely, since it has no link with recovery
Look at the weekly average, since HRV is noisy from day to day
e: HRV picks up a problem earlier than morning heart rate, but it is noisy day to day, so use a weekly average.

q: A client's fatigue, low mood and falling performance have persisted even after you cut their training load. What do you do?
o: Refer them to a GP
Cut the load further until the symptoms clear
Raise the load, since the drop may have caused the low mood
Diagnose overtraining syndrome from their resting heart rate
e: No single marker diagnoses overtraining, and it is a medical diagnosis of exclusion. If symptoms persist after the load is cut, refer to a GP.

q: A client wants to take an ice bath after every lifting session to help them grow. What do you tell them?
o: It makes no difference either way, so it does not matter
It is probably counterproductive for growth
It is the best-evidenced way to speed up muscle growth
It helps growth only if taken before the session
e: The inflammatory response to lifting is part of the signal for adaptation, and regular ice baths straight after may blunt growth, though the evidence is thin. Cold immersion is useful for feeling functional quickly between competitions or two sessions in a day.

q: A client's progress stalls during a stressful month at work. How do you read it?
o: As a plateau, to be broken by raising the load
As a sign the programme was badly designed from the start
As an adherence problem, to be fixed with firmer accountability
As shared load: life and training stress draw on one capacity
e: A programme that works in a calm month will fail in a bad one. That failure is not an adherence problem and should not be treated as one.

q: A client asks how many hours of sleep they need to recover from training. What do you tell them?
o: Ten hours for anyone training more than three times a week
Six hours is enough for most people who train
No magic number: eight hours is a working shorthand
Exactly eight hours for every adult who trains
e: Sleep needs vary. Quality counts too: darkness, a cool room, bright light in the morning and dim light in the evening.

q: A client says 'I feel like everyone is staring at me.' Which barrier is this?
o: Lack of social support
Ambivalence
Convenience
Social physique anxiety
e: Social physique anxiety is worry about how one's body looks to others. Encourage comfortable clothing, find quieter areas and offer other ways to take part.

q: A client with depression says they cannot start exercising until their flat is tidy and their life is more organised. What is the right approach?
o: Design the programme so the barrier cannot bite
Treat it as ambivalence and talk through the costs of sitting still
Set tidying the flat as their first process goal
Agree to wait until they have tidied and feel organised
e: Where a barrier comes from the client's condition rather than a gap in knowledge, design around it. Asking a depressed client to tidy their room first is asking them not to be depressed.

q: A client says: 'When my 12:30 meeting ends on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, I will change and walk to the gym.' What is this?
o: An implementation intention
Coping planning
Technique imagery
Self-monitoring with a training log
e: An implementation intention is an if-then plan tied to a specific cue. Coping planning anticipates barriers and makes other plans in advance.

q: A client says negative thoughts about their body keep interrupting their sessions. Which approach is best supported?
o: Tell them to ignore it and push on
Use appearance imagery to picture their ideal body
Teach them to say 'stop' out loud whenever it appears
Help them reframe the thought
e: Thought-stopping is poorly supported and can make unwanted thoughts return more often. Reframing the thought works better.

q: A client's technique has gone on a set, but they insist they can do another rep. Whose call is it?
o: Yours: end the set
Theirs, as long as they stay within their target reps in reserve
Yours, but only if they are still a beginner
Theirs: they know their own body best
e: If a client insists on another rep after technique has gone, that is your call, not theirs.

q: A client mentions new back pain that has started waking them at night. What is the right response?
o: Carry on as normal while the pain stays under 5 out of 10
Add core work, since the pain suggests weak stabilisers
Train around it, avoiding the movements that hurt
Refer for a diagnosis
e: 'We are not trying to bring a fitness solution to a medical problem.' Pain that is new, severe, worsening, unexplained or at night needs a diagnosis. Known, settling pain in a cleared client can be trained around.

t: Readiness, and the stages of change
q: A client says 'I eat fine, it doesn't really matter' and jokes whenever the subject comes up. Which approach fits?
o: Start a food diary to show them what they are really eating
Curiosity: ask how they feel about their current habits
Ask which one change they feel ready to make this week
Give them detailed information about the risks of their diet
e: This is precontemplation. Information alone rarely helps and can reinforce disengagement; the question to ask is 'How do you feel about your current habits?'

t: Readiness, and the stages of change
q: A client says 'I know I should, but...' and reads about exercise without starting. What helps most at this stage?
o: Resolving ambivalence without forcing a decision
A demanding outcome goal, to create a sense of urgency
A detailed weekly plan built on implementation intentions
Waiting for the action stage before discussing any barriers
e: This is contemplation. Detailed planning does not suit it; validate both sides, review barriers that have come up and plan together for when they return.

q: You ask a client how important a change is to them on a scale of 1 to 10, and they say 6. What do you ask next?
o: 'Why isn't it a 10?'
'Would you like me to explain why it should be higher?'
'Shall we wait until it is at least an 8?'
'What would need to happen for that 6 to become a 7?'
e: Scaling questions turn a yes or no into a direction of travel, and the follow-up question does the work.

q: A trainer says: 'It sounds like part of you is ready, and another part still has questions.' Which OARS skill is this?
o: A summary
An affirmation
An open-ended question
A reflection
e: Reflections show empathy and understanding. Affirmations reinforce strengths, summaries capture motivations, and open questions invite reflection.

q: You want to refer a client to a dietitian. Which wording frames the referral best?
o: 'You need to see a specialist about this, not me.'
'This would get you something more tailored than I can give.'
'I can't help you with this any more, I'm afraid.'
'This is beyond what I can do, so you need to see someone.'
e: Frame referral as support, a way to gain more personalised tools, not as escalation or a response to failure. It is the same referral, heard quite differently.

q: A client holds a belief about food that you think is mistaken. What does validating their experience mean?
o: Correcting the belief firmly before discussing anything else
Avoiding the subject of food with them from then on
Acknowledging their experience as real, without agreeing with every belief
Agreeing with the belief so that the working relationship is not damaged
e: Validating someone's experience does not mean agreeing with every belief or behaviour. That answers the usual objection to client-centred language.

q: A client says they have no discipline because they eat half a jar of peanut butter standing at the counter most evenings. How do you approach it?
o: As an environment problem: plate it and sit down
As a character problem, to be fixed by building stronger willpower
As a knowledge problem, by explaining the calories in peanut butter
As a reason to cut out all spreads from their diet permanently
e: A client who says they have no discipline usually has an environment problem, and the environment is the thing that can be changed.

q: What is stimulus control?
o: Rewarding the client with something they value after each session
Saying 'stop' out loud whenever an unwanted urge appears
Logging every meal and snack to spot the triggers over time
Changing the environment so the unwanted behaviour is harder
e: Stimulus control is a core part of behavioural weight programmes, though its effect on its own is hard to isolate. Its rules: decide once in advance, make the default the thing you want, and a boundary can be physical.

q: A client wants chocolate, but a healthy dinner they normally love does not appeal at all. What does that suggest?
o: Low blood glucose that needs sugar
A need to log all food for a week
A craving rather than physical hunger
Genuine physical hunger for energy-dense food
e: Physical hunger makes most food appealing; a craving is specific. Someone who wants chocolate but not dinner is not hungry.

q: A client with binge eating disorder asks whether urge surfing could help them. What is the right response?
o: Use HALT instead, since it is the safer first tool
Teach it, checking again after 15 to 20 minutes each time
Start detailed food logging so the binges can be tracked
Refer, since riding the urge is not enough here
e: Do not use either technique for everyone. For binge eating disorder the situation is a referral, not a technique problem.

q: Roughly how heritable is BMI in twin studies?
o: Roughly 15 to 25%
Over 90%
Roughly 40 to 70%
Roughly 5 to 10%
e: BMI is among the more heritable common traits. The evidence is against treating obesity as mainly a matter of knowledge or choice.

q: A client says their weight is entirely down to their own lack of willpower. How do you respond?
o: Agree, and set stricter rules to build their willpower
Explain the structural causes of their weight in detail
Suggest they start once their willpower has improved
Decline the willpower frame
e: You do not need a theory of why a client is the size they are. 'Here is what we can change in this room' is not the same as 'this is why you are here', and only the second blames them.

q: What is the practical core of weight-neutral practice?
o: Weighing clients weekly but never telling them the result
Measuring success by something other than the scale
Never discussing food or eating with a client at all
Holding that weight loss is never achievable or appropriate
e: It measures success by behaviour, fitness, blood markers and wellbeing rather than the scale. The strong version, that weight loss is never achievable or appropriate, is contested; the practical stance survives on adherence grounds alone.

q: A client works shifts, has two young children and says they cannot cook from scratch. How do you treat that?
o: As a reason to give them a strict meal plan
As excuses to push through with better planning
As real constraints to design around
As a sign they are not ready to change
e: Time, money, kitchen access, shift patterns and childcare are real constraints. Shift work, several jobs, commuting and childcare use up the time the usual advice assumes.

t: Questions to ask about any diet
q: A client is about to start a very restrictive diet they read about. Which question is most useful to ask?
o: 'How fast would you like to lose the weight on it?'
'Can you see yourself doing this the rest of your life?'
'Who was it that recommended this diet to you?'
'How many calories a day does this particular diet give you?'
e: If the answer involves never eating birthday cake again, rethink the approach. These are motivational interviewing questions: the answers come from the client.

t: Questions to ask about any diet
q: Why ask a client 'Do you want to keep the weight off once you lose it?'
o: It names the real goal and makes speed a cost
It screens them quietly for a possible eating disorder
It shows how motivated they are, on a scale from 1 to 10
It lets you calculate their target calorie intake for the week
e: Once keeping the weight off is the stated goal, a fast diet becomes a cost. Then ask 'what can we tweak?', a soft word chosen on purpose.

t: Reading a scale with a client
q: A client is upset that the scale shows 1 kg more than yesterday. What do you tell them?
o: Read the weekly average, not a single reading
Cut their calories a little today to correct the gain
Recalculate their calorie targets straight away
Weigh them again this evening to confirm the gain
e: Weight is a piece of data, not a measurement of success or failure. Weigh often and read the weekly average, or do not weigh at all if it upsets the client.

t: Reading a scale with a client
q: How long must weight stay the same before you treat it as a plateau and recalculate?
o: Three to four days
One week
Three to four weeks
Three months
e: Only after three to four weeks at the same weight is it a plateau. Over a few days fluid swings swamp the signal.

q: A client has started and stopped exercising several times before. How do you set their goals?
o: An ambitious outcome goal first, to create urgency
Process goals first, each with a floor for bad days
Outcome and process goals together, with no allowance for bad weeks
No goals at all until they have trained for three months
e: Put process goals first while confidence is the limit. A floor keeps the record of completed weeks unbroken, so the programme never fully stops and never has to be restarted.

q: 'Run a 10K race within a year' is which kind of goal?
o: An implementation intention
An outcome goal
A sub-goal
A process goal
e: An outcome goal is the final achievement. Process goals are the daily and weekly steps, such as jogging an hour three days a week plus two training sessions.

q: A client asks you why their knee hurts on the stairs. Which of these is outside your scope?
o: Suggesting lifestyle changes
Diagnosing the cause of the knee pain
Giving general nutritional information
Carrying out an individual movement assessment
e: Diagnosing or treating pain or disease is outside scope. Assessment, programme design, general nutrition information and lifestyle suggestions are within it.

q: How is a fitness professional's scope of practice mainly set in the US?
o: By the rules of neighbouring professions
By the certifying body's own rules alone
By federal law written specifically for personal trainers
By the liability waiver that each client signs
e: Fitness professionals in the US and many other countries have no specific government regulation, so their scope is set by neighbouring professions.

q: In Germany, a healthy adult asks you to set macros for fat loss. Is that within your scope?
o: Yes, but only if the sessions are billed to a Krankenkasse
Yes: it is permitted and is not Heilkunde
No: only a Diätassistent may set macros for anyone
No: nutrition advice of any kind needs a Heilpraktiker
e: In Germany the line is between a healthy person and a patient, not between advice and no advice. Anything billed to a Krankenkasse is restricted to approved providers.

q: In Germany, a client with diagnosed coeliac disease asks you to manage their diet. What is the position?
o: Permitted, since Ernährungsberater is not a protected title
Restricted: it is therapy, so refer
Permitted, provided you declare it to your insurer first
Permitted, if they sign a consent form beforehand
e: Ernährungstherapie, the dietary treatment of a disease, counts as Heilkunde and needs a doctor, a Heilpraktiker or a Diätassistent.

q: A client you are giving macro targets to tells you they have just been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. What changes?
o: Nothing, since the macros were already agreed
You need only a signed consent form to carry on
It moves closer to therapy, so refer
You should lower their carbohydrate target yourself
e: The risk is rarely the job title; it is the client. A disclosure of type 2 diabetes, thyroid disease, an eating disorder or pregnancy turns general advice into something closer to therapy.

q: A client asks you to write them a full weekly meal plan. Staying within your scope of practice, what do you do?
o: Write it, since meal planning counts as general nutrition advice
Refuse to discuss food or eating with them at all
Decline the meal plan, but share general healthy meal options
Write it, provided they have no diagnosed medical condition
e: Prescribing meal plans is outside a trainer's scope of practice. The line is whether you are making an individual clinical judgement: a plan attached to one person's body is practice.

q: A client's persistent fatigue has not improved despite sensible changes to food, sleep and training. What do you do?
o: Refer, since it is a referral trigger
Change the nutrition plan again and review in a month
Recommend a supplement to raise their energy
Cut their training volume and wait another month
e: This is the trigger most likely to be missed, because it has no diagnosis attached. Persistent fatigue may signal hormonal, metabolic or mental health concerns.

q: You are worried a client has an eating disorder: they have added sessions and were upset about missing one. How do you raise it?
o: Name the behaviour you have seen and offer a referral
Comment gently on how much weight they seem to have lost
Say you will stop training them until they get help
Tell them you think they have anorexia and need help
e: Name a behaviour, never their body or weight. Do not diagnose, name a disorder or make training conditional; losing contact helps nobody.

q: A client you are worried may have an eating disorder asks for a body-fat measurement to track progress. What do you do?
o: Do not weigh, measure or assess body composition
Use bioelectrical impedance, since it is quick
Use skinfolds, since they are more private than a scale
Measure, but do not tell them the result
e: Skinfolds, BIA and scale weight can all do harm, and the assessment itself can become part of the disorder.

q: During your outdoor session in Germany, a stranger nearby collapses. What is your legal position?
o: You must wait for emergency services rather than give care
You may help, but you are fully liable for any harm caused
You have no duty to help a stranger, only your own client
You must help, and you are protected when you do
e: In Germany, failing to help where help is necessary and reasonable is a criminal offence under §323c StGB, and §680 BGB limits a helper's liability to intent and gross negligence.

t: Blood pressure and the Valsalva manoeuvre
q: A client with high blood pressure holds their breath and strains on a heavy leg press. What happens when they release the breath?
o: Blood pressure returns smoothly to its resting value
Blood pressure stays low for several minutes afterwards
Blood pressure overshoots above baseline for several beats
Blood pressure falls, but only in clients on medication
e: During the strain less blood returns to the heart and pressure falls; on release blood floods back and pressure overshoots before settling. In someone with high blood pressure or heart disease that spike is the mechanism behind the cardiac events, which is why the cue is to breathe out on the effort.

q: You are planning outdoor winter sessions for a client. Why ask first about exercise-induced asthma?
o: Warm, humid air is its most common trigger
Cold, dry air is its most common trigger
Air pollution is its most common trigger
High pollen counts are its most common trigger
e: Cold, dry air is the most common trigger; pollution, high pollen and airborne chemicals also trigger it. Clients prone to it should take precautions before exercising outdoors.

q: What is the mechanism of exercise-induced asthma?
o: A fall in blood oxygen caused by low fitness
Weakness of the diaphragm under heavy breathing load
Spasm of the intercostal muscles during hard breathing
Bronchospasm, plus inflammation and mucus
e: Bronchospasm is tightening of the smooth muscle around the airways. The symptoms are coughing, wheezing and shortness of breath.

q: A client arrives with a fever and aching muscles but wants to train. What do you do?
o: Train as normal if they took paracetamol
Train lightly, keeping the intensity well down
Train hard to sweat the virus out
Rest, and return gradually once it has passed
e: Exercise during a viral heart infection (myocarditis) can be dangerous and is hard to rule out at home. Exercise does not burn off a virus or flush out toxins.

q: A client says they are always ill and blames the programme. What should you consider?
o: Only two of the five factors are about training
They need more training to build up their immunity
The programme must be too hard, so halve it straight away
Moderate training raises infection risk above sedentary levels
e: The five are exposure to germs, suppression after hard exercise, poor diet, mental stress and lack of sleep. The answer may not be the programme.

t: Exercising a client on glucose-lowering medication
q: A client on insulin seems unusually shaky, sweaty and confused after a set. What should you consider?
o: Dehydration, so give them water and continue
Simple tiredness, so give them a longer rest
Hypoglycaemia, which is easily mistaken for exertion
Low motivation, so encourage them through the next set
e: Shakiness, sweating, confusion and weakness all look like exertion, which is why hypos get missed. They should carry fast-acting carbohydrate, and you should know where it is.

t: Exercising a client on glucose-lowering medication
q: How often should you ask a client on a sulphonylurea about their medication, when they last ate and any previous hypos?
o: Only if they look unwell
Once, at intake
Once a month
Before each session
e: Ask before each session, not once at intake. The risk also lasts hours past the session, so it does not end when they leave.

q: A cleared client with known patellar tendinopathy reports knee pain of 3 out of 10 during split squats that settles by the next morning and is not building week to week. What is the right call?
o: Refer them immediately, as for any pain at all
Continue, but only if they take painkillers first
Continue, monitoring the pain
Stop all lower-body work until the pain has gone
e: In a cleared client with a known condition, pain up to about 5 out of 10 is acceptable if it settles by the next morning and does not build week to week.

q: A cleared client's known Achilles pain is only 3 out of 10 during sessions, but it has been a little worse each week for three weeks. What is the right call?
o: Continue, since the pain is still under 5 out of 10
Push on, since tendons need progressive load
Continue, since it settles by the next morning
Refer, because it is worsening
e: The rule has three parts: up to about 5 out of 10, settling by the next morning, and not building week to week. Refer for new, severe, worsening, unexplained or night pain.

q: A client with knee osteoarthritis asks whether exercise or medication should come first. What does NICE guidance say?
o: Rest first, then exercise once the joint has settled
Medication first, with exercise once the pain is controlled
Surgery first, then exercise as rehabilitation
Exercise first, ahead of medication
e: In NICE guidance, exercise is the first-line treatment for knee and hip osteoarthritis, ahead of medication.

q: What programme suits a client with knee osteoarthritis?
o: Strengthening plus aerobic work, with the pain-monitoring rule
Stretching only, to protect the joint
Aerobic work only, avoiding any strengthening that loads the knee
Strengthening only, and no aerobic work until pain settles
e: Use strengthening plus aerobic work, with weight loss where it applies. Supervised sessions help clients keep going.

q: Midway through a session, a client in an uncomplicated pregnancy mentions one of these. Which means you stop?
o: Her heart rate has passed 140 beats a minute
A headache that will not settle
She is breathing harder but can still talk in sentences
She feels more tired than she did before pregnancy
e: The stop signs are vaginal bleeding or fluid leak, chest pain, dizziness, a headache that will not settle, calf pain or swelling, contractions or reduced movement of the baby. Intensity is judged by the talk test, not a heart-rate cap.

q: A 68-year-old with osteoporosis and a past vertebral fracture wants to start. Which is the right starting point?
o: Sit-ups and toe touches to strengthen the spine
Progressive strength work, with impact at brisk-walking level
Walking only, since strength work is unsafe with osteoporosis
High-impact jumping, since that is how impact builds bone fastest
e: Progressive strength and impact work is recommended, but after a vertebral fracture keep impact to brisk-walking level. Avoid loaded, repeated or end-range bending and twisting such as sit-ups, toe touches and loaded rotation.

q: An older client wants to cut their risk of falling. What makes a falls programme effective?
o: Chair-based exercise that avoids any risk of losing balance
Machine strength work twice a week, leaving balance out
Daily walking, since walking is natural balance training
Balance work that truly challenges them, about 3 hours a week
e: Exercise cuts falls in older adults by about a quarter, mostly through balance and functional work. WHO advises balance and strength activity on three or more days a week.

q: On average, when is peak height velocity?
o: About 15 in both
About 11.5 in girls and 13.5 in boys
About 9 in girls and 11 in boys
About 13.5 in girls and 11.5 in boys
e: The growth spurt begins at about 9 in girls and 11 in boys; peak height velocity follows at about 11.5 and 13.5. Growth slows and stops about two years after it.

q: A parent says their 10-year-old's big improvement this year proves the training is working. What is the more accurate account?
o: Mostly muscle growth produced by the training itself
Almost entirely better diet at that age
Mostly growth and maturation, with a neural training effect
Almost all training, since children change little before puberty
e: A training effect exists before puberty, mostly the nervous system coordinating fibre firing better. After puberty, improvement is the training.

q: What is the relative age effect?
o: Late maturers end up shorter than early maturers as adults
Children train better alongside others of the same biological age
Children born early in the selection year are selected more often
Older adults respond more slowly to the same training
e: In football as many as 50% of selected children are born in the first three months of the selection year, and as few as 10% in the last three.

q: A coach calls an early-maturing 11-year-old the most talented player in the squad. What is the accurate reply?
o: Early maturers should be moved up an age group straight away
The advantage is largely size, not talent
Late maturers rarely reach a similar adult height
Early maturity reliably predicts elite adult performance
e: Selection systems reward biological age and call it talent, and the advantage then fades. Performance before puberty is a poor guide to adult potential.

t: Training young people: what to do
q: A parent asks whether strength training is safe for their 10-year-old. What do you tell them?
o: Unsafe before puberty, because lifting damages growth
Safe when properly prescribed and supervised
Safe only as competitive weightlifting under a federation
Safe, and it will build noticeable muscle within months
e: The 2014 International Consensus and the NSCA both support it. Start with body weight and technique; before puberty the gains are neural. What the American Academy of Pediatrics opposes is the competitive lifting sports.

t: Training young people: what to do
q: A 13-year-old in the middle of the growth spurt is struggling to learn a new skill. What do you do?
o: Drop strength work and focus on hard conditioning instead
Ease off skill learning and keep strength work going
Push through with extra skill practice before the window closes
Stop all training until the growth spurt is over
e: The spurt disrupts coordination, so pushing through trains faults. Watch for knee and heel pain, and do not overlook the late maturers.

t: Training young people: what to do
q: You start coaching a 14-year-old privately in Germany. Which precautions apply?
o: Parental consent and first aid; record checks are for clubs only
Consent from the child, and messaging them directly to plan sessions
An erweitertes Führungszeugnis, parental consent, no closed doors
A medical clearance form, and a closed room for their privacy
e: Clubs must check the enhanced criminal record certificate under §72a SGB VIII, and it is good practice when self-employed. Also communicate through parents and agree a photo policy.

q: Where does early specialisation in one sport work?
o: In any sport at all, provided the training is supervised
In baseball, where early specialisers win more scholarships
In football, where early selection predicts adult success
Where peak performance comes in adolescence
e: Examples are women's gymnastics and figure skating; it also works for winning in your own age group now. Otherwise the evidence favours sampling several sports.

q: Roughly how much sport time should go to play and other sports before age 12, according to the deliberate-play research?
o: About 20%
About 50%
About 80%
About 5%
