e: The rough allocation is about 80% before 12, falling to 50% between 13 and 15, and 20% after 16.

q: What is the status of the claim that 70% of children quit organised sport by 13?
o: It is accurate but applies only to football
It has no traceable source
It understates the true figure of about 90%
It comes from a large, well-run cohort study
e: Children do often switch or leave sports around 12, but the 70% figure has no traceable source.

q: Among children who leave a sport, what is the most common reason?
o: The cost of taking part
Injury, which accounts for most who leave
The coach, teammates or environment
Feeling not good enough at the sport
e: Over 70% leave because of the coach, teammates or environment; injury accounts for about a quarter and feeling not good enough for 15%. Retention depends on the relationship before the programme.

q: What is the evidence for the age windows in long-term athlete development models?
o: Little: animal research stretched to cover human motor skill
Moderate: the windows hold for speed but not for strength
Strong for girls, but weak for boys
Strong: several controlled trials show the windows in children
e: Most fitness qualities can be trained at any point in childhood. Use the ages as a default structure, never as a test of normal development.

q: A parent worries that their 12-year-old has missed the 'window' for developing speed. What do you tell them?
o: It is true: speed can no longer be developed at 12
Speed can be developed only once puberty is complete
The window is a planning convention, not a deadline
They should start intensive speed training now to catch up
e: Most fitness qualities can be trained at any point in childhood. The ages in LTAD models are a default structure, never a test of whether a child is developing normally.

q: A study reports a relative risk of 2.0 for one group. What does that mean?
o: Half the risk of the baseline group
Twice the risk of the baseline group
The same risk as the baseline group
A 2% higher risk than the baseline group
e: A relative risk compares a group with a baseline set at 1.0: 2.0 means twice the risk, 0.5 half.

q: Going from under 10 to 10 to 29 minutes of activity a day takes relative risk of depression from 1.00 to 0.82. What does 0.82 mean?
o: An 82% lower risk than the baseline group
An 18% lower risk than the baseline group
An 18% higher risk than the baseline group
0.82 percentage points lower than the baseline group
e: The baseline is set at 1.0, so 0.82 is 82% of the baseline risk, which is 18% lower.

q: How does low fitness compare with smoking as a risk of death, adjusted for age?
o: Roughly twice the relative risk of smoking
A slightly higher relative risk than smoking
Exactly the same relative risk as smoking
About half the relative risk that smoking carries
e: In women it is 2.23 against 2.12, in men 2.03 against 1.89. BMI is the weakest of the major factors, roughly half the risk of low fitness.

q: Inactivity has the lowest risk ratio of the four major risk factors. Why does it still cause the most disease?
o: Its risk ratio is underestimated in every study
Far more people are inactive than smoke
Inactivity is also the main cause of smoking
It interacts with BMI to double its own risk
e: A weaker risk carried by three times as many people does more total harm.

q: Moving from the least fit to the second-least fit fifth of the population cuts all-cause mortality by how much?
o: About 15%
About 5%
Over 50%
Nothing, until the top fifth is reached
e: The largest health gain available to anyone is the step from doing nothing to doing a little.

q: What is a session for with a very deconditioned client?
o: Moving them off the bottom of the curve, not making them fit
Making them fit as quickly as possible
Preparing them for vigorous training within a month
Mainly teaching technique, since the health benefit comes later
e: They capture most of the benefit before they would describe themselves as someone who exercises, which is a much smaller ask.

q: A 60-year-old says there is no point starting, since they have been unfit all their life. What do the data say?
o: Only people who were fit when young benefit from training
Starting late is nearly as protective as having been fit and losing it
Starting late is more protective than staying fit throughout life
Starting late gives no measurable benefit to the risk of death
e: Unfit to fit carried a relative risk of 0.52, fit to unfit 0.56, against 1.00 for staying unfit. Current behaviour beats history.

q: Against 1.00 for staying unfit, roughly what relative risk of death does staying fit carry?
e: Fit to fit was 0.33, unfit to fit 0.52 and fit to unfit 0.56, against 1.00 for unfit to unfit. Becoming fit late is nearly as protective as having been fit and losing it.

q: An overweight, unfit client has exercised regularly for two months and the scale has not moved. What do you tell them?
o: They must be eating more than they are reporting to you
The programme has failed and needs replacing entirely
Expected at first, and their health risk is still falling
Exercise has no health benefit without some weight loss
e: Someone overweight and unfit cannot yet train hard or long enough to burn much, so nothing happens on the scale for one to three months. They still get the lower risk of heart disease, diabetes, some cancers and death from all causes.

q: A heavier client has heard that 'fitness beats fatness'. For which outcome does this not hold?
o: All-cause mortality in women
Mortality in heavier people who exercise
All-cause mortality in men
Type 2 diabetes
e: Fitness beats fatness for mortality, in both sexes. For type 2 diabetes BMI is an enormous driver: a woman at BMI 27 to 28.9 carries about 16 times the risk, and above 35 over 90 times.

q: A client on blood-pressure medication says training has lowered their readings and they want to stop the tablets. What do you say?
o: Halve the dose for a few weeks and see how they feel
Keep training, since the effect is permanent after a few months
Raise it with their GP; the decision is the doctor's
Stop the tablets, since exercise works as well as medication
e: Never encourage a client to reduce or stop medication. The blood-pressure effect also reverses within a month of stopping training.

q: In patients with coronary disease, what exercise dose was linked with regression of existing plaque?
o: Any activity above 150 minutes in a month
About 2,200 kcal a week, roughly 35 km of walking
Three 20-minute sessions a week, as for mortality
One long walk of an hour or more each week
e: Three 20-minute sessions a week captured the mortality benefit; reversing arterial disease took roughly ten times that. Keep the two doses apart.

q: In the Diabetes Prevention Program, what did 7% weight loss plus 150 minutes of activity a week do to diabetes incidence in people with prediabetes?
o: Had no effect beyond metformin
Cut it by 58%, against 31% for metformin
Cut it by 31%, against 58% for metformin
Cut it by about 10%, the same as metformin
e: Prediabetes is the stage where exercise still prevents rather than manages.

q: A client with type 2 diabetes refuses to do any cardio. Can they still get the glucose benefit?
o: Only if they also manage to lose 10% of their weight
Only on the day of each session, not over the weeks
No: only aerobic training has any effect on blood glucose
Yes: strength training raises insulin sensitivity too
e: A single bout lowers blood glucose that day, and regular training raises insulin sensitivity over weeks. Both aerobic and strength training do it.

q: A client is going through chemotherapy and wants to keep training. What is the right approach?
o: Treat their fatigue as deconditioning and progress hard
Clearance, the treating team informed, and defensive goals
Wait until treatment has ended before any exercise at all
Tell them exercise will help to treat the cancer itself
e: Chemotherapy affects blood counts, heart function and bone, and treatment fatigue is not deconditioning. Never imply exercise treats the cancer.

q: For cancer-related fatigue, what did a meta-analysis of 113 studies find?
o: Exercise and psychological help worked; drugs did not
Drugs helped most, and exercise made little difference
Rest helped most, and exercise made fatigue worse
Nothing tested made a measurable difference
e: The authors say clinicians should prescribe exercise first. It is the strongest form the 'exercise is medicine' claim takes, from a direct comparison.

q: Which of these is secondary ageing, and so largely avoidable?
o: Osteoporosis
A decline in body awareness
A decline in reaction time
A decline in VO2max
e: Primary ageing is the built-in decline in VO2max, muscle, bone density, reaction time, memory and body awareness. Secondary ageing is disease, much of it avoidable.

q: What are the three overlapping parts of successful ageing?
o: No disease, no medication and no pain at all
Strength, flexibility and balance, trained in that order
Low disease and disability, good function, engagement with life
Low body weight, a high VO2max for their age and a good memory
e: Staying engaged with life sits equal with the other two, and it describes what an older client is protecting.

q: What dose of aerobic exercise roughly halved depression and tension scores in the study given?
o: One 10-minute session a week, over four weeks
Daily sessions of 90 minutes or more, over six months
Five hour-long sessions a week, over a whole year
Two sessions a week of 20 to 30 minutes, over 12 weeks
e: The dose is small. That is not a scaled-down version of real training; it is the intervention that was studied.

q: A client under GP care for depression read that exercise beat medication for relapse and wants to stop their antidepressants. What do you say?
o: Stop the medication, since relapse was 8% against 38% on tablets
Stop once they are training three times a week
Their GP decides; the study says nothing in favour of stopping
Halve the dose while their training increases
e: A trainer never advises on medication and never implies exercise is an alternative to treatment. The trainer provides the exercise alongside the GP and therapist.

q: A client you train alongside their depression treatment mentions feeling hopeless and having thoughts of suicide. What do you do?
o: Suggest yoga, since it is among the best tolerated
Add an extra session, since exercise reduces symptoms
Note it and raise it at their next review
Refer immediately, not train through it
e: Hopelessness and suicidal thinking are on the symptom list and are an immediate referral, not something to train through.

q: A client has tight hip flexors and weak glutes. Must glute strengthening wait until the hip flexors have been released and stretched?
o: No: that rule is a preference, not a requirement
Yes: strengthening into a restriction does not work
Yes: the continuum order has been shown to be necessary
No: the glutes should always be strengthened before release
e: NASM's rule is to inhibit and lengthen overactive tissue before activating underactive tissue. Full-range strength training improves range about as much as stretching, so treat the rule as a preference.

q: With a layered crossed presentation, where do you begin?
o: The hip flexors and lumbar extensors
The feet and ankles, working upwards through the chain
The neck and shoulders, working downwards
Wherever the client feels the symptom most
e: Easing strain at the core reduces how much you have to do further out. The restriction is rarely where the symptom is.

q: Midway through a session, a client says their calf has become painful and it looks swollen. What do you do?
o: Carry on while the pain stays under 5 out of 10
Stretch the calf gently and move to upper-body work
Stop the session and get them medical help
Switch to cycling to keep the calf moving
e: Calf pain with swelling is on the stop-and-act list, with chest pain, breathlessness out of proportion to effort, dizziness or confusion, palpitations, sudden severe headache and new weakness or numbness. The 5 out of 10 rule is for known, settling pain in a cleared client.

q: A client with a sore lower back says their hamstrings feel tight and asks you to stretch them hard. How is the tightness best framed?
o: It is causing the pain, so stretching it comes first
It is often the response to pain rather than its cause
It shows overactive tissue, so roll it before anything else
It means the fibres are short and need lengthening
e: Pain makes muscles guard, which is the opposite of what corrective work is for, and tightness is often the response to pain. Pain overrides every rule of the continuum.

q: A client rolling their calves says the pressure is 9 out of 10 and they are gritting their teeth. What do you change?
o: Roll faster so the pressure feels less intense
Ease off to about 6 or 7 out of 10, then hold
Keep going, since higher pressure gives a faster release
Stop rolling the calves for good
e: Find the tender spot by rolling along the muscle, aim for 6 or 7 out of 10, never higher, then stop and hold until the tension drops by roughly half. 20 to 30 seconds is the minimum to get a response.

q: A client with controlled high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes asks whether foam rolling is safe for them. What is the accurate reply?
o: Neither is a contraindication in expert consensus
Rolling is safe for them only with a vibration roller
Both rule out rolling of any kind entirely
Rolling is safe only once they are off medication
e: In an international expert consensus, only open wounds and fractures reached agreement as contraindications. NASM's own list is far longer than the consensus supports.

q: A client with osteoporosis would benefit from upper-back self-myofascial work. How do you adapt it?
o: Roll lying on the floor, but for a shorter time
Leave it out, since osteoporosis rules out any kind of rolling
No rolling over the spine or ribs; use a ball on a wall
Roll the spine, but with the softest roller available
e: Osteoporosis is a modify, not an avoid. Do not roll over bony regions, and age alone is not a contraindication.

q: What is NASM's dose for static stretching?
o: Hold for 30 seconds, one to three repetitions, daily
Hold for 15 seconds, five repetitions, three times a week
Hold for 10 seconds, three to five repetitions, twice a week
Hold for 2 minutes, once, daily
e: Take the muscle passively to the point of tension, never past it, and hold for 30 seconds, one to three times, daily.

q: A client wants to stretch after every session to reduce next-day soreness. What do you tell them?
o: Stretching afterwards is the best way to prevent soreness
Stretching afterwards makes the soreness worse
They should stretch before the session instead
It does not reduce soreness
e: Static stretching is not a recovery tool and does not reduce soreness (well supported). Before a session it is corrective and assessment-driven.

q: In the kneeling hip flexor stretch, a client loses their posterior pelvic tilt as soon as the arm goes overhead. What do you do?
o: Drop the pelvic tilt so the arm can go higher
Add a side bend to take them further
Keep the arm up and push them deeper into the stretch
Stop at the previous layer
e: Each layer is a place to stop. Forcing through a pattern is renting it; controlling it is owning it.

q: In the layered kneeling hip flexor stretch, what comes straight after setting up the half kneeling position?
o: Rotating the trunk towards the front leg
A posterior pelvic tilt, tucking the pelvis under
Reaching overhead with the arm on the down-knee side
Drawing in at maximum effort
e: The order is half kneeling, then posterior pelvic tilt, then drawing in at 10 to 15% effort, then reaching overhead on the down-knee side, side bending and rotating.

q: Which combined stretch suits a lower crossed presentation?
o: A standing gastrocnemius and hip flexor stretch facing a wall
A kneeling lat stretch with the forearms resting on a ball
A supine hamstring stretch with a strap around the raised foot
A seated adductor stretch on a ball, legs wide
e: Both hands go on the wall with the trunk upright. It combines two regions in one position.

q: A combined gastrocnemius and hip flexor stretch is claimed to affect the head and shoulders. What is the status of that claim?
o: Untested: it has not been studied
Disproven by several randomised trials
Established for the superficial front line only
Well supported by dissection studies
e: The claim rests on the myofascial lines, and treating one end to affect the other is untested (little evidence).

q: A client finds overhead movement troublesome. Which activation exercise is the first choice?
o: Robbery, elbows back into external rotation
Standing salute with a loop band
Chicken wings in a supine bridge
Wall slide, forearms on the wall sliding up
e: The wall slide trains the overhead pattern and is the first choice for troublesome overhead movement.

q: Where do you start a client who needs scapular control work?
o: Swimming, hovering one arm before any reach
A full side plank on the hand rather than the elbow
Chicken wings combined with a supine bridge
Leg pull prone with the hands well ahead of the shoulders
e: Swimming is the starting point, hovering only before any reach. The elbow side bend is the regression for the lateral chain, and chicken wings are high-level work.

q: Where should the band go for crab walks targeting gluteus medius?
o: Around the feet
Around the waist
Around the thighs
Around the knees
e: The evidence favours the band at the feet rather than higher. The client hinge squats with the hands forward in line with the shoulders.

q: A client has overpronation. Which activation exercise fits?
o: Crab walks with the band around the knees
A kneeling lunge for the hip flexors
Intrinsic foot strengthening
Cobra, following psoas release
e: Intrinsic foot strengthening targets the foot intrinsics and is listed for overpronation and Morton's foot.

q: Why are the developmental positions, from supine up to half kneeling, useful training tools?
o: They follow the order in which adult muscles switch on
They lengthen the muscles more than stretching does
Each is a harder stability problem than the one before
Repeating the infant sequence fixes adult dysfunction
e: The positions are fairly well supported as training tools. The evidence is against the idea that repeating the infant developmental sequence fixes adult problems.

q: What does the tall kneeling position test?
o: Ankle mobility and foot control, with the knees unloaded
Hip extension and pelvic control, without the ankles
Thoracic extension and shoulder support
Rotation, with no need for stability
e: Tall kneeling takes the ankles out: knee, hip, shoulder and head in a vertical line with the belt line level. Periscope tests rotation, sphinx thoracic extension.

q: What is NASM's dose for dynamic stretching?
o: One set of 10 repetitions, across 3 to 10 exercises
Three sets of 15 repetitions, across 2 exercises
Two sets of 20 repetitions, across 5 different exercises
One set of 30 repetitions, of a single exercise
e: One set of 10 across 3 to 10 exercises, such as prisoner squats, multiplanar lunges with reach, leg swings and high knees.

q: A football coach asks whether a structured dynamic warm-up is worth the time. What does the evidence say?
o: It helps only if followed by long static holds
It raises injury risk in unfit players
It cuts football injuries by about 39%
It makes no measurable difference to injury rates
e: The FIFA 11+ result is well supported in football. A dynamic warm-up suits almost everyone, scaled in range and speed.

q: When does load go on to a movement?
o: Only after a set number of weeks of corrective work
From the first session, to build confidence
Once the client asks for it
Once the pattern is owned
e: Load goes on once the pattern is owned. Loading a rented pattern conditions the compensation.

q: Where should a client's hips start in a deadlift?
o: As low as possible, as in a squat
Wherever the bar, shin and shoulder set-up puts them
As high as possible for every lifter, whatever their build
Level with the knees for everyone
e: Hip height depends on arm, leg and trunk length. The cue 'hips as high as possible' targets the reverse-squat error, but the set-up is the better guide.

q: How is NASM's resistance playlist of 45 exercises organised?
o: By pattern, from least stable to most stable, then power
By muscle group, from the smallest to the largest
By equipment, from machines through to free weights
Alphabetically, with no progression running through it
e: Once you see that order you can work out the regression and progression for any exercise, including ones nobody demonstrated.

q: A client wants to squat close to their maximum while standing on a balance device. What do you tell them?
o: Yes, once they have trained on the device for a month
No: never use balance devices for near-maximal lifts
Yes, as long as a spotter is standing by
Yes: it is the best way to build strength and balance together
e: An unstable surface reduces force output, so loading heavily on one gives less force and more risk. Heavy loads call for stable environments such as benches and machines.

q: On an unstable surface, what is the training stimulus, and what does it cost?
o: The extra volume, and it costs recovery
The extra load, and it costs balance
The slower tempo, and it costs range
The instability itself, and it costs load
e: Base stability and load move in opposite directions: you can have an unstable base or a heavy load, but not both. Make the trade deliberately.

q: A new client with no health issues wants to start lifting. Must they pass through a stability phase before strength work?
o: Yes: NASM's phase order has been shown to be necessary
No: the order is proven only for clients with poor posture
No: nothing shows that a stability phase is needed first
Yes, for at least four weeks of stabilisation work
e: NASM's phases are an organising scheme. Nothing shows a client must pass through them in order.

q: A client owns the kettlebell deadlift hinge. When can they start two-hand swings?
o: Only after a stabilisation block of single-leg hinges
Only once they can deadlift double their swing bell
Only after completing all of the strength phases
Early: the power column is not a gate
e: The kettlebell course teaches the swing straight after the deadlift. Single-arm and double-bell swings are the advanced end.

q: What do NASM's master instructors recommend as a replacement for direct trap work, although NASM's library omits it?
o: Barbell shrugs
Face pulls
Upright rows
Loaded carries
e: The library has no carries, no anti-rotation or Pallof press, no kettlebell work, almost nothing in the hinge pattern, and nothing for rotation at Phase 1.

q: What do NASM's instructors use as their main substitute for the Russian twist?
o: Loaded seated rotation with a plate
Weighted sit-ups on a decline bench
Anti-rotation, such as the Pallof press
Side bends holding a heavy dumbbell
e: They use anti-rotation across all five phases, even though NASM's library does not include it.

t: Is the exercise at the right level?
q: On a single-leg cable row, a client's knee drifts inwards on most reps at the planned tempo. What do you do?
o: Keep going, since the instability is the stimulus
Regress one dial, such as a split stance
Swap it for a completely different exercise
Add load, which will stabilise the knee
e: The test is whether the client can hold all five kinetic-chain checkpoints for every rep at the planned tempo. If not, regress one dial, not the whole exercise.

q: A client's squat technique breaks down on the last two reps at the target reps in reserve. What do you change?
o: Drop the load by 10 to 20%, or regress one dial
Keep the load and push for the full set
Add two more reps to build endurance
Add load, since the client is clearly working hard
e: Technique breaking calls for less load or one dial down. Too easy at the target RIR calls for more reps, then load; pain calls for a change of range, load or exercise.

q: A client has ten minutes and only wants more range of motion. Should they both roll and stretch?
o: No: do one, as the pair adds no range
Yes, but stretching must come before rolling
No: neither technique improves range at all
Yes: combining them doubles the range gained
e: A 2021 meta-analysis found the combination does not improve range over either technique alone. Combine them when performance work follows.

q: A client will do both rolling and stretching before a performance session. In which order?
o: Rolling, then stretching
Either order gives the same result
Stretching, then rolling
Alternating one minute of each
e: The combination beats either technique alone for performance, but only as rolling then stretching.

q: What are the three steps of the lift-specific warm-up?
o: General cardio, dynamic mobility, then ramp-up sets
Static stretching, foam rolling, then working sets
Ramp-up sets, dynamic mobility, then general cardio
Twenty minutes of cardio, then straight into working sets
e: General cardio for 5 to 10 minutes raises temperature, then dynamic mobility for the day's patterns, then ramp-up sets. This follows the RAMP structure, and a short RAMP warm-up takes about 10 to 12 minutes.

q: A client's working weight on the squat is 100 kg. How might you run their ramp-up sets?
o: Straight to 100 kg for a single, then working sets
Three sets of 10 at 60 kg
Empty bar only, then working sets
Empty bar, then about 50, 70 and 85 kg
e: The example is empty bar, then 50%, 70% and 85% of working weight. The percentages are coaching convention, not a tested protocol.

t: Static holds before a maximal effort
q: A client likes to stretch before a heavy single. Can they?
o: Yes, but only after the heavy single
No: any static stretching before a maximal effort ruins it
Yes, kept short and followed by the dynamic work
Yes, with holds of at least two minutes per muscle
e: Shorter holds inside a dynamic warm-up make little or no difference. Holds totalling about 60 seconds or more per muscle just before a maximal effort can reduce force slightly.

t: Static holds before a maximal effort
q: Holds totalling about 60 seconds or more per muscle are done just before a maximal effort. What is the effect on force?
o: It rises slightly, because the muscle is primed
It falls slightly
It falls so much that stretching before lifting is ruled out
It is unaffected, however long the holds
e: Long holds tested straight away can reduce force slightly, which is why the claim that static stretching impairs performance is overstated. Shorter holds inside a dynamic warm-up make little or no difference.

q: Which of these is an external cue?
o: 'Push off the ground.'
'Push off your feet.'
'Straighten your knees.'
'Squeeze your glutes.'
e: An internal cue points attention at the body; an external cue points it at the effect on something outside it. Almost every cue NASM teaches is internal.

q: What did a 2024 re-analysis that corrected for publication bias find about external focus cues?
o: External cues harm learning in beginners
External cues give a moderate benefit for most tasks
Internal cues are better for learning a new skill
The average effect is close to zero
e: Earlier meta-analyses favoured external cues, but the corrected average is close to zero, with wide variation. Use whichever cue works for the client.

q: On a glute bridge, the work keeps drifting to the client's hamstrings. What cue do you use?
o: An external cue: 'push the floor away'
An internal cue: 'squeeze the glutes'
A tempo cue: 'go faster'
No cue, just more reps
e: When raising activation in one muscle is the goal, keep the cue internal. Internal focus raises EMG activity in the target muscle, and dropping it lets the movement drift.

q: You are teaching a client the kettlebell swing as a new pattern. Which kind of cue do you try?
o: External
Internal
Internal first, then external once the pattern is learned
An attachment-point cue naming the glutes' two ends
e: Try an external cue when the goal is the movement rather than the muscle: anything loaded, fast, skilled or being learned as a pattern.

q: A client's hips keep sagging in a plank. Which external cue fits?
o: 'Squeeze your abdominals as hard as you can.'
'Draw your navel in towards your spine.'
'Tuck your chin in and hold it there.'
'Keep your belt buckle pointed at the wall ahead.'
e: The belt buckle cue stops the hips sagging without naming a muscle.

q: A client's head keeps drifting forward during rows. Which cue fixes neck position most reliably?
o: 'Eyes on a spot on the floor two metres ahead.'
'Tuck your chin in throughout the set.'
'Keep your head stacked right over your shoulders.'
'Lengthen through the back of your neck.'
e: Gaze is genuinely external and easy to check from across the room. It works better than asking for a chin position the client cannot feel.

q: On a dumbbell fly, a client keeps bending the elbows to bring the hands together. What cue do you use?
o: 'Bring your hands together.'
'Lift the weights higher.'
'Press the upper arms together.'
'Squeeze your hands into the dumbbells.'
e: A muscle can only pull its two ends together. Pec major runs from the sternum to the humerus, so cueing the upper arms moves the insertion towards the origin; the hand is not one of its ends.

q: What is 'keep a pen between your shoulder blades' a cue for, and why does it work?
o: Neck position, by fixing the gaze
Scapular retraction, in one image
Shoulder elevation, as a fully external cue
Thoracic rotation, by naming the muscle
e: The image replaces retract, depress, hold and do not shrug. It is only weakly external, which does not matter for activation work.

q: When should you reach for an analogy cue?
o: Only with advanced lifters who know the terms
Before any other cue, on every exercise
When the position has several parts to hold at once
Only where an internal cue would be appropriate
e: One image beats four instructions, wherever it sits on the internal and external scale. Reach for an analogy before a third cue.

t: Changing the task instead of cueing
q: A client cannot feel whether their spine is neutral in a hinge, however you cue it. What do you do?
o: Switch to a vague image of a straight line
Keep repeating 'neutral spine' until it clicks
Lay a dowel along their back
Remove the hinge from the programme
e: Keep three points of contact: head, mid-back and tailbone. Some positions have no real external version, so change the task so the position happens on its own: the constraints-led approach.

t: Changing the task instead of cueing
q: Why does a constraint beat a cue whenever one is available?
o: It allows heavier loads to be used straight away
It gives continuous feedback and costs no attention
It raises activation in the target muscle most
It lets the client ignore the position entirely
e: The dowel, the tape line, the band round the knees and the wall behind the heels all correct the position without words.

q: A beginner has just done a set with some good reps and some poor ones. Which reps do you comment on?
o: None, to avoid overload
The ones that went well
The ones that failed
Every rep in turn
e: Beginners already know which reps failed and want to hear about the good ones. Experienced people want to hear about the ones that did not go well.

q: How much should you say immediately before a rep?
o: Nothing at all
Three cues, one per joint
Every cue that applies
A single cue
e: Talk as much as you need during the working phase, but the last thing said before the rep is one cue. Set a performance bandwidth so not every rep needs correcting.

q: Which cueing claim is better replicated?
o: Internal focus raises target-muscle activation
External focus improves performance for everyone
Analogy cues outperform every other kind of cue
Internal focus adds extra muscle growth
e: Internal focus raising target-muscle activation is better replicated than any growth benefit built on it, which rests on one small trial.

q: The external versions of NASM's internal cues, such as 'keep your belt buckle pointed at the wall', have what evidence behind them?
o: A meta-analysis of external-focus cueing studies
Randomised trials comparing each cue with its original
NASM's own cue sheets and instructor testing
None directly: they are built by reasoning
e: They are constructed from the principle, not quoted from a source or tested in studies. Judge them on whether they work on a real person.

t: What the practice reference does not cover
q: What is the evidence for sinew channels and acupressure points such as SI5, KI7, BL60 and GB38?
o: Moderate, from small trials of pressure-point release
Strong for pain relief, weak for range of motion
Weak, from a single positive trial
No credible evidence base
e: There is no supporting research, which is why the practice reference leaves this material out.

t: What the practice reference does not cover
q: A client with no medical clearance mentions a sore shoulder they have never had assessed. Can you train around it?
o: Yes, if the pain is under 5 out of 10
No: that is a referral
Yes, if it settles by the next morning
Yes, by avoiding overhead work
e: Working around pain is for cleared clients. Pain with no clearance, or pain that is new, severe, worsening, unexplained or at night, is a referral.

t: The swing, and its three errors
q: At the top of each swing, a client leans back and arches the lower back. What is the fix?
o: Finish tall and neutral, ribs down
Have them lift the bell with the arms instead
Place a foam roller between the feet
Cue them to lift the chest higher at the top
e: Finish with the hips and knees extending together and the glutes tight. Overextension is often driven by coaching that demands chest height; the foam roller between the feet fixes a different error, the squatty swing.

t: The clean, the rack, and hand insertion
q: In the kettlebell rack, a client's elbow floats away from the body and their shoulder is working hard. What do you correct?
o: Rest the elbow on the hip, bone on bone
Lift the elbow higher to keep the bell off the forearm
Grip the handle harder to hold the bell still
Hold the bell further away from the body
e: Lift the elbow and the weight shifts forward, so the shoulder starts working for no reason. The rack is the rest position.

t: The clean, the rack, and hand insertion
q: A client with a long torso and short arms cannot get comfortable in a two-bell rack. How do you read it?
o: As a lack of effort they need to push through
As a mobility problem that stretching will fix
As a fact about their proportions
As a sign they need heavier bells to settle it
e: A short torso with long arms makes the two-bell rack simple; a long torso with short arms may rule it out. That is a fact about bodies, not a failure of effort.

q: For isolation work such as flies, presses and curls, which implement is the better tool?
o: The kettlebell
Either, with no difference
The dumbbell
Neither: only machines suit isolation
e: A kettlebell's offset weight allows ballistic work; for isolation the balanced dumbbell is better. Match the implement to the goal.

t: Start with the constraint, not the exercises
q: A new client says they would like to train five days a week, but their schedule suggests two. What do you build from?
o: The exercise list first, then fit the days around it
What they will actually do, which sets everything else
Three days, as a compromise
Five days, to stretch them
e: Ask what they will actually do, not what they would like to do. The common error is to start at the exercise list and discover the constraint afterwards.

t: Start with the constraint, not the exercises
q: What is the binding constraint when designing a client's week?
o: The client's training age and past experience
Days available multiplied by session length
The client's recovery capacity between sessions
The number of exercises the trainer wants to include
e: It is almost always set by the client's life, not by physiology.

t: What the evidence supports (session and week)
q: A client asks whether a body-part split builds more muscle than full-body training. What do you tell them?
o: Splits build clearly more muscle than full body
Full body builds clearly more muscle than splits
They produce equivalent results when volume is equal
Splits build more strength but less muscle
e: A 2024 systematic review found them equivalent when volume is equal. Splits may make higher volume easier to sustain, which helps indirectly.

t: What the evidence supports (session and week)
q: A strength-focused client asks whether training a lift more often per week helps. What does the evidence say?
o: Once a week is best for strength
Frequency matters only for muscle growth
Frequency makes no difference to strength once volume is equal
Frequency does increase strength, with diminishing returns
e: For growth, frequency mainly distributes volume. For strength it helps, with diminishing returns: this is where the two goals diverge.

t: Effort: RPE and reps in reserve
q: On the lifting RPE scale, what does RPE 9 mean?
o: About three reps left
About one rep left
No reps left
About two reps left
e: RPE 10 is no reps left, RPE 9 about one and RPE 8 about two.

t: Effort: RPE and reps in reserve
q: A new client finishes a set of 15 and rates it RPE 8. What should you bear in mind?
o: They probably have more left than they think
RPE applies only to sets of 5 reps or fewer
Beginners overestimate what they have left, so they are at failure
RPE is meaningless for beginners, so ignore it
e: Most people underestimate what they have left by about one rep, more so in high-rep sets, so teach the scale early.

q: A client on 3 sets of 8 to 12 at 2 reps in reserve gets 12, 12 and 10 reps. What do you do next session?
o: Add a fourth set at the same load
Drop the load so that every set reaches 12
Add the smallest load step now
Keep the same load for now
e: Double progression keeps the load until every set reaches the top of the range at the target reps in reserve.

q: A client on 3 sets of 8 to 12 reaches 12 on every set at the target reps in reserve. What do you do?
o: Add the smallest load step and drop back to 8 reps
Keep the load and add reps up to 15
Keep everything the same for another two weeks
Add a large load jump and stay at 12 reps each set
e: Once every set reaches the top of the range, add the smallest load step and return to the bottom of the range.

q: A client's attendance is genuinely unpredictable. Which split fits best?
o: A body-part split, for short sessions
Push/pull/legs over three days
Upper/lower over four days
Full body
e: For unpredictable attendance, full body is the right option, not just the beginner option. With a body-part split a missed day means a muscle group misses a week.

q: A client with three days a week suggests push/pull/legs. What is the drawback?
o: The sessions become far too long to sustain
It needs four days to reach twice-weekly frequency
It leaves no room for any compound lifts
Each muscle is trained only once a week
e: At six days push/pull/legs is the best structure for high volume per muscle. At three it is only reasonable if frequency is not the priority.

t: The order to decide things in
q: You have chosen a split that fits the days a client will train. What do you check next?
o: The rest periods for each set
The exact exercises for each muscle
The client's one-rep maxes
Pattern coverage across the week
e: After the days and the split, check pattern coverage against the placement table, then order within the session with the tier method. A week missing vertical pulling is obvious; one missing 'lats' is not.

t: The order to decide things in
q: A client who is now used to plyometrics wants to do them regularly. What dose do most studies use?
o: Two a week, with a day or two between them
Daily sessions, each of low volume
One session every 7 to 14 days
Four sessions a week on consecutive days
e: Seven to fourteen days applies only after a first, unfamiliar, highly damaging session. Once the client is used to it, the repeated bout effect shortens recovery.

q: A client can train only two days a week. What is the compromise, and how do you manage it?
o: None: two days easily reaches 10 hard sets per muscle
Total volume: pick compounds, minimal isolation
Intensity: keep every load light throughout
Frequency: train each muscle once a week with a split
e: Two days rarely reaches 10 sets per muscle. Rotating which session comes first means neither is always trained on the more tired day.

q: A two-day client has a shoulder that does not tolerate overhead pressing. What do you do with the vertical push?
o: Replace it with a 'safe' overhead variation at a lighter load
Replace it with an extra lower-body exercise to keep sessions short
Keep it in, but with a lighter load and a slower tempo
Take it out, and add horizontal pushing and pulling
e: An irritable shoulder usually needs more pulling anyway. Add rotator cuff work at tier 3 and keep the carries.

q: A two-day client's shoulder refuses overhead pressing. Should vertical pulling stay in the programme?
o: Yes, if it is painless: test it rather than assuming
Yes, but only with heavy loads
No: replace it with shrugs
No: overhead pulling always aggravates such a shoulder
e: Many shoulders tolerate pulling overhead while refusing to push there.

q: A Romanian deadlift was dropped because a straight bar hurt the client's wrist, and a leg extension was put in its place. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
o: The client should push through the wrist pain with a lighter bar
Nothing: the leg extension trains the same muscles
The leg extension should be swapped for a leg curl
The hinge was lost; restore it with a wrist-friendly implement
e: A leg extension is knee-dominant, so the pattern was lost, not substituted. Options include a plate-loaded back extension, a cable pull-through, a dumbbell or trap-bar RDL, or a barbell RDL with straps.

q: A client is training for a kettlebell sport competition. Which bell should they train with?
o: The bell they will compete on
Any cast iron bell
Whichever bell the gym has
An adjustable bell, to save money
e: Bells look alike and behave differently. Sport bells keep the same dimensions from 8 to 48 kg.

q: Your commercial gym has mismatched kettlebell brands and no pairs. What gives the client a better return?
o: Using only the heaviest bell
Dumbbells
Swinging mismatched pairs
Buying a sport bell
e: Commercial gyms rarely stock a usable range. In that setting a dumbbell gives a better return on the time invested.

t: The squat, and why the pickup differs
q: Which kind of kettlebell suits the goblet squat better?
o: Sport or competition
Adjustable
None: goblet squats need a dumbbell
Cast iron
e: The goblet squat is the entry point, and cast iron suits it better. It is also what most gyms and clinics have.

t: The squat, and why the pickup differs
q: In a single-bell rack squat, the client's free arm drifts out to the side. What do you do?
o: Nothing: it is normal counterbalancing
Cue them to keep the arm pinned to their side
Give them a second bell to balance it
Switch to a lighter bell straight away
e: This is the unbalanced version of the squat, and the opposite side works hard. A heavier load pins the arm back.

q: Why prefer the half snatch to the full snatch?
o: It uses more grip, which builds forearm strength
It is faster and more aggressive on each rep
It keeps the bell close, saving the hands and grip
It skips the rack, so there is less to learn
e: A half snatch goes up in one motion, then down into the rack before the next rep. The full snatch is faster and harder on the grip.

q: A client wants to snatch two bells. Which version do you use?
o: The full snatch with the bells rotated over the top
The full snatch, since it is faster
Either, as long as the load is light
Always the half snatch
e: A double full snatch drops a lot of load from overhead onto the lower back and hips.

q: A client has only 15 minutes. Why might a clean and squat complex suit them?
o: It isolates the quadriceps for the whole session
It covers pulling and pushing patterns in little time
It is a single pattern, so it can be loaded more heavily
It rests the upper body completely while the legs work
e: Complexes cover a lot of patterns in very little time, which is why they suit short sessions. The clean and squat covers upper and lower body pulling, then a lower body push.

q: A client finds the jerk too technical. What are the alternatives for getting overhead?
o: A snatch, which replaces the jerk
The push press or the strict press
There are none, since the jerk is required
Only a seated press from the floor
e: The jerk is the fastest way overhead and the most technical push, but it is not required.

q: A client over 1.8 m tall trains in a room with a low ceiling and cannot press overhead standing. What do you use?
o: Kneeling variations
Heavier bells
Standing presses with a bent arm
Full snatches
e: Ceiling height is one of two practical reasons for kneeling and seated variations. Swing, clean, snatch and half snatch all work from the knee.

q: A client trains at home with only light bells. How can kneeling help?
o: It makes seated presses easier
It lets them lift much heavier bells than standing
It doubles the load on the hips
Taking the hips out makes a light bell hard
e: Kneeling takes the hips out of the movement, which extends the useful life of the bells you own.

q: What does a ladder of 1, 2, 3 repeated for five rounds give you over 3 sets of 10?
o: Fewer total reps, which suits a deload week
The same 30 reps, never more than three at a time
Twice the total reps in the same amount of time
Longer sets, which build muscular endurance
e: The client also chooses their own rest. A ladder to 3 is heavier; 3-4-5 moderate; 4-5-6 lighter.

q: A client doing a 20-minute container has gone from four rounds to eight. When do you increase the load?
o: Never: keep adding rounds instead
Only once they reach twelve rounds
Once the round target is met
Every session, by 2 to 4 kg
e: Do not increase the load until the round target is met. Then build again from four rounds.

t: Regressions for a larger or deconditioned client
q: Why are high-rep swings a poor fit for a larger, deconditioned client?
o: They are too easy to progress, so the client soon stalls
Swings do not train the hip extensors, only the lower back
The bell has nowhere to go, and heart rate climbs near maximum
They can only be done safely with an expensive sport bell
e: Start with short sets on RPE and the talk test, and build. Ballistic work comes later, as conditioning improves.

t: Regressions for a larger or deconditioned client
q: A larger client finds the full range of a kettlebell deadlift too much. What is the right regression?
o: Raise the bell on a block or step to reduce the range
Assist by pulling the bell up for them on each rep
Remove the deadlift from the programme entirely
Replace it with high-rep swings
e: A yoga block is about 10 cm, an aerobic step or box 15 to 30 cm. Raising the load reduces the range while the client still does all the work.

q: A client who does not compete asks what shoes to wear for kettlebell training. What do you suggest?
o: Weightlifting shoes with a raised heel
Running shoes with plenty of cushioning
Any shoe, since footwear makes no difference
Flat, hard-soled, zero-drop shoes, or barefoot
e: Weightlifting shoes with a raised heel on a hard surface are for competing. Most kettlebell equipment is for competition.

q: A client learning the clean wants kettle guards for forearm bruising. What do you say?
o: Never use them, as they ruin technique
Use them only together with a belt
Fine at first, but do not rely on them
Essential for every session, permanently
e: Forearms toughen and technique improves, so the guards become unnecessary.
